lessons.title: Comprehension, Simple Present Simple Past
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their reading comprehension skills and learn how to recognise and use the simple present and simple past tenses.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding how punctuation can change the meaning of a sentence
✔ Reading short comprehension passages carefully
✔ Retrieving information directly from a text
✔ Identifying descriptive words
✔ Sequencing events and instructions
✔ Finding words and phrases with similar meanings
✔ Making sensible predictions from information in a text
✔ Understanding what a verb is doing within a sentence
✔ Recognising the simple present tense
✔ Recognising the simple past tense
✔ Understanding when the simple present tense is used
✔ Understanding when the simple past tense is used
✔ Identifying verbs describing regular routines and general facts
✔ Identifying verbs describing events that have already happened
✔ Choosing missing verbs to complete sentences
✔ Using context to decide whether a sentence is in the present or past tense

Students begin by exploring how punctuation can completely change the meaning of a sentence. They then work through a series of short comprehension activities involving a princess, a bus and a story about Jack and a cow. Students retrieve information, identify vocabulary, sequence events and make sensible predictions using evidence from each passage.

The lesson then introduces the simple present and simple past tenses through familiar situations. Students describe their normal morning routine using present-tense verbs such as wake, brush, eat and wear before describing activities that have already happened using past-tense verbs such as watched, played and talked.

Students then apply their tense knowledge through an interactive butterfly challenge. They complete missing verbs including forgot, grow and choose and use the meaning of each sentence to decide whether it is written in the simple present or simple past tense.

By the end of the lesson, learners will have strengthened their comprehension skills and be able to distinguish between simple present and simple past verbs, understanding how each tense is used according to when an action happens.

lessons.title: Comprehension with Transitioning Exercises
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop a wide range of English skills through comprehension, creative writing, grammar, spelling and vocabulary activities.

This lesson includes:
✔ Reading and answering comprehension questions
✔ Retrieving information from fiction and non-fiction texts
✔ Understanding the purpose and effect of a text
✔ Sequencing events in the correct order
✔ Rewriting descriptions using adventurous vocabulary
✔ Using exciting sentence starters
✔ Exploring friendship and relationships through reading
✔ Reading and retrieving information about the history of chocolate
✔ Using conjunctions correctly
✔ Using the past tense
✔ Adding commas to lists
✔ Creating expanded noun phrases
✔ Developing stronger and more interesting vocabulary
✔ Recognising the suffixes -ly and -ful
✔ Practising Year 1 and Year 2 common exception spellings

Students begin with an All About Me activity before improving a jungle description in their own words, using adventurous vocabulary and stronger sentence starters to make the setting vivid and engaging.

The lesson then develops comprehension skills through a timed reading activity about the speed of sound and a series of texts about friendship. Students retrieve information, identify vocabulary in context, sequence events and use evidence from the text to explain their answers.

Students also read about the history of chocolate, answering questions about cacao, the Aztecs, Christopher Columbus, Hernán Cortés, early chocolate houses and the development of chocolate production.

Grammar and vocabulary activities include choosing appropriate conjunctions, working with past tense sentences, punctuating lists with commas, developing expanded noun phrases and replacing ordinary adjectives with more ambitious alternatives.

Students finish by exploring the suffixes -ly and -ful through a hidden-picture activity and correcting twelve misspelt common exception words.

By the end of the lesson, learners will have strengthened their comprehension, grammar, spelling and vocabulary skills while building confidence across a broad range of Year 3 English activities.

lessons.title: Similes and Metaphors
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how similes and metaphors can make writing more vivid, imaginative and powerful. They explore how figurative language creates pictures in the reader’s mind and practise using it to improve their own descriptions.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding what similes are and how they use like or as
✔ Creating similes from pictures and descriptive prompts
✔ Using ambitious adjectives alongside similes
✔ Improving sentences with stronger descriptive language
✔ Understanding metaphors and how they differ from similes
✔ Identifying metaphors in sentences, poetry and prose
✔ Exploring metaphors from The Highwayman by Alfred Noyes
✔ Explaining the effect of figurative language on the reader
✔ Creating metaphors to describe people, body parts and everyday objects
✔ Using animal metaphors to add power and personality
✔ Choosing metaphors to add description, interest and mood
✔ Applying similes and metaphors independently in creative writing

Students begin by exploring familiar similes and creating their own comparisons using like and as. They then combine adjectives and similes to transform simple sentences into more vivid descriptions and develop ambitious vocabulary through descriptive activities.

The lesson then introduces metaphors and examines how direct comparisons differ from similes. Students explore a range of familiar metaphors before studying examples from The Highwayman and discussing how carefully chosen figurative language can create powerful images and atmosphere.

Students develop their own metaphors for people, body parts, objects and animals, considering how each comparison can add description, interest or power to a sentence.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to recognise, explain and create effective similes and metaphors and use them confidently to make their own writing more descriptive, imaginative and engaging.

lessons.title: Present Perfect Tense
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to recognise, form and use the present perfect tense and understand how it differs from the simple past tense.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding when the present perfect tense is used
✔ Recognising the difference between past and present perfect tense
✔ Forming the present perfect tense using has or have
✔ Using past participles correctly
✔ Changing sentences from the past tense to the present perfect tense
✔ Understanding actions that began in the past and continue into the present
✔ Recognising past actions that still have an effect in the present
✔ Choosing correctly between has and have
✔ Working with regular and irregular verbs
✔ Identifying past participles such as grown, done, been and forgotten
✔ Matching past tense verbs with their present perfect forms
✔ Selecting the correct tense according to context and timing
✔ Applying tense knowledge to sentences, recounts and reasoning activities

Students begin by learning how the present perfect tense is formed using has or have with the correct past participle. They practise changing past tense sentences into the present perfect and explore regular and irregular verb forms such as ate and eaten, broke and broken, grew and grown, and did and done.

The lesson then develops students’ understanding of when each tense should be used. They learn that the simple past describes events that started and finished in the past, while the present perfect can describe something that began in the past and continues now or something whose result is still important in the present.

Students practise identifying and correcting verb forms, matching past and present perfect sentences, changing a football recount into the present perfect tense and choosing the correct tense according to the context of a sentence.

Finally, students explore auxiliary verbs and past participles in greater depth, learning when to use has or have and recognising irregular forms such as done, come, forgotten, blown, begun and drawn.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to distinguish between the simple past and present perfect tense, form the present perfect accurately and select the appropriate tense according to meaning and timing.

lessons.title: Articles A, AN & THE
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to choose and use the articles a, an and the correctly, as well as recognising situations where no article is needed.

This lesson includes:
✔ Recognising vowels and consonants
✔ Choosing between a and an according to the sound of the following word
✔ Understanding why sound rather than spelling determines whether to use a or an
✔ Using a before consonant sounds and an before vowel sounds
✔ Recognising exceptions such as a unicorn, a university and an hour
✔ Choosing articles when adjectives appear before nouns
✔ Understanding the as the definite article
✔ Using the to refer to a specific person, animal, place or thing
✔ Distinguishing between general and specific references
✔ Recognising situations where no article is required
✔ Using articles correctly with countable and uncountable nouns
✔ Using a or an when introducing something and the when referring to it again
✔ Using articles correctly with rivers, lakes, mountains, mountain ranges, islands and countries
✔ Using the with superlatives
✔ Recognising when institutions such as school and university take no article
✔ Applying article rules accurately within sentences and longer passages

Students begin by revising vowels and consonants before learning the basic rules for a and an. They discover that the sound at the beginning of the following word is more important than its first written letter, explaining why we say a unicorn and a university but an honest person and an hour.

The lesson develops this understanding through sorting, sentence-completion and error-correction activities. Students also explore how adjectives affect the choice of article, comparing examples such as an enormous cat and a delicious egg.

Students then learn about the definite article the and how it identifies a particular person, animal, place or thing. They compare general and specific references and learn how a noun may first be introduced using a or an and then referred to again using the.

The lesson extends into more advanced article rules, including when no article is needed and conventions for geographical names, countries, institutions and superlatives. Students apply these rules to examples involving rivers, lakes, mountains, mountain ranges and country names.

Finally, students consolidate their learning through a challenge in which they choose between a, an, the or no article across a wide variety of contexts.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to choose a, an and the accurately, recognise when no article is required and apply article rules confidently according to sound, meaning and context.

lessons.title: Word families
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students explore word families and learn how words can be connected through roots, prefixes, suffixes, word forms and meaning.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding what word families are
✔ Identifying common roots within groups of words
✔ Exploring how prefixes and suffixes change words
✔ Understanding morphology and how words are built
✔ Exploring roots such as struct and spect
✔ Understanding prefixes such as tri and over
✔ Sorting words into different word families
✔ Identifying odd words that do not belong in a word family
✔ Combining roots, prefixes and suffixes to form real words
✔ Recognising related nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs
✔ Exploring words ending with common suffixes such as -tion
✔ Understanding synonyms and antonyms
✔ Developing vocabulary through related words
✔ Selecting appropriate word-family members to complete sentences

Students begin by examining familiar word families such as help and write before learning how roots, prefixes and suffixes connect words through their structure and meaning. They explore examples such as triangle, tricycle and tripod to understand how the prefix tri relates to the meaning three.

The lesson then investigates the roots struct and spect. Students generate their own examples before exploring how struct is associated with building, arranging or putting things together, while spect is connected with looking and seeing.

Students practise sorting jumbled words into families including vent, cover, uni and graph, identify odd-one-out words and combine prefixes, roots and suffixes to create genuine words such as inspect, repress, invent, venture, respect, pressure, replace and placement.

The lesson then broadens the idea of related words by exploring different grammatical forms of the same root, common spelling patterns, prefixes, synonyms and antonyms. Students investigate how nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs can all belong to the same wider word family.

Finally, students apply their understanding in a sentence-completion quiz, choosing related words such as driver and driving, solve and solution, player and replay, and hurt and hurtful according to their meaning and grammatical role.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to recognise and build word families, identify relationships between words and use their understanding of roots, prefixes, suffixes and word forms to develop their vocabulary.

lessons.title: Descriptive writing
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their descriptive writing skills by exploring how carefully chosen vocabulary and figurative language can create vivid and engaging images for the reader.

This lesson includes:
✔ Using interesting and precise adjectives
✔ Choosing powerful verbs
✔ Using adverbs to describe actions
✔ Creating effective similes
✔ Using metaphors to build vivid imagery
✔ Recognising and creating alliteration
✔ Using personification to bring descriptions to life
✔ Developing and improving descriptive vocabulary
✔ Writing extended descriptive passages

Students begin by revising important word classes used in descriptive writing. They identify nouns and explore how adjectives can add detail and help the reader picture a person, place, animal or object more clearly.

Students are encouraged to move beyond simple adjectives such as big, nice, beautiful, small and old, replacing them with more precise and imaginative vocabulary such as enormous, stunning, tiny and ancient.

The lesson then explores verbs and adverbs. Students identify suitable action words for a scene and add carefully chosen adverbs to explain how those actions are taking place.

Students will:
✔ Identify nouns, adjectives, verbs and adverbs
✔ Select more ambitious vocabulary
✔ Match powerful verbs to nouns within a scene
✔ Add adverbs to give actions greater detail
✔ Use vocabulary choices to create clearer images for the reader

The lesson then introduces a range of descriptive writing devices. Students learn that similes compare one thing with another using words such as like or as, while metaphors describe something as though it actually is something else.

Students also explore alliteration, where nearby words begin with the same sound, and personification, where human characteristics or actions are given to something non-human.

Students will:
✔ Create original similes
✔ Develop effective metaphors
✔ Recognise and use alliteration
✔ Use personification to make settings feel alive
✔ Combine figurative language with carefully selected vocabulary

Students then bring these techniques together in an extended descriptive writing task based on a beach scene. They are encouraged to write at least two or three paragraphs containing interesting adjectives, powerful verbs, carefully selected adverbs, similes, metaphors, alliteration and personification.

Further activities require students to focus closely on one object, person or animal and create a detailed description of it. They also review their own vocabulary and use a thesaurus to improve weaker word choices.

Students then apply the same descriptive techniques to another setting, such as a town centre, a busy market or the first day of school.

The lesson finishes by analysing a short descriptive passage and identifying examples of verbs, adverbs, adjectives, personification, alliteration, metaphor and simile.

By the end of the lesson, students will confidently use a range of vocabulary and figurative language techniques to make their descriptive writing more vivid, imaginative and engaging.

lessons.title: Plurals and Pronouns
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of singular and plural nouns and explore how pronouns and alternative nouns can be used to avoid unnecessary repetition in writing.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding the difference between singular and plural nouns
✔ Forming regular plurals by adding s or es
✔ Applying plural rules to nouns ending in ch, sh, s, ss, x and z
✔ Forming plurals of nouns ending in y
✔ Recognising when y changes to ies
✔ Exploring nouns ending in f or fe that change to ves
✔ Recognising irregular plurals such as foot and feet
✔ Recognising nouns such as sheep that remain unchanged in the plural
✔ Understanding what pronouns are and how they replace nouns
✔ Identifying personal, possessive, relative and reflexive pronouns
✔ Using pronouns to avoid repetition
✔ Using alternative nouns to make writing smoother and more varied
✔ Identifying pronouns within sentences
✔ Rewriting repetitive sentences and passages
✔ Using pronouns clearly so the reader knows which noun they refer to
✔ Using demonstrative pronouns such as this, that, these and those

Students begin by learning the difference between singular and plural nouns and exploring the spelling rules used to change nouns from one to more than one. They practise adding s and es, changing consonant-plus-y endings to ies and exploring exceptions such as loaf becoming loaves, foot becoming feet and sheep remaining sheep.

The lesson then introduces pronouns as words that can take the place of nouns. Students explore a range of personal, possessive, relative and reflexive pronouns, including he, she, it, they, mine, yours, who, which, that, myself and themselves.

Students identify pronouns in sentences before replacing repeated nouns with suitable pronouns. They then improve increasingly challenging sentences and passages by combining pronouns with alternative nouns, learning that repetition should be reduced without making it unclear who or what a pronoun refers to.

Further activities require students to construct their own sentences using selected pronouns and alternative nouns. They apply these skills to different picture prompts involving visitors, tourists, swimmers and competitors.

The lesson finishes with a demonstrative pronouns quiz focusing on this, that, these and those. Students use singular and plural context to select the correct pronoun and complete each sentence accurately.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently form a range of regular and irregular plurals, recognise and use different types of pronouns, reduce unnecessary repetition and select appropriate demonstrative pronouns according to meaning and number.

lessons.title: Standard English and Compound Words
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of Standard English and compound words, learning how to recognise and correct non-standard forms and how words can be combined to create compound nouns with new meanings.

This lesson includes:
✔ Recognising the difference between Standard and non-standard English
✔ Correcting non-standard verb forms and expressions
✔ Using was and were accurately
✔ Choosing correct past tense forms such as saw and did
✔ Using have correctly instead of expressions such as should of and could of
✔ Distinguishing between commonly confused words such as borrow and lend
✔ Avoiding double negatives and informal expressions in formal writing
✔ Editing sentences, conversations and passages into Standard English
✔ Understanding what compound nouns are
✔ Combining words to create compound nouns
✔ Recognising open, closed and hyphenated compound nouns
✔ Understanding how compound words can develop new meanings
✔ Exploring how spoken stress can affect meaning
✔ Forming plurals of compound nouns correctly
✔ Identifying the important word within a compound noun when forming plurals
✔ Creating new compound nouns and definitions
✔ Building compound words from pictures and word clues

Students begin by comparing Standard English with forms that may occur in informal or regional speech. They correct examples such as we was to we were, I done it to I did it, I seen him to I saw him and should of to should have. They also explore vocabulary choices such as borrow and lend, our and are, and those and them within Standard English sentences.

Students then apply these skills to increasingly challenging material, correcting non-standard English within individual sentences, conversations, advertisements and a longer written extract. They learn to identify inappropriate verb forms, slang, double negatives and other constructions and replace them with suitable Standard English alternatives.

The second part of the lesson introduces compound nouns. Students learn that two or more words can combine to create a noun and that compound nouns may be written as one word, as separate words or with hyphens. They explore examples including football, steam train, armrest, handful and mother-in-law and learn to check unfamiliar spellings when necessary.

Students investigate how combining words can change meaning, comparing examples such as greenhouse and green house, redhead and red head, boyfriend and boy friend, and homework. They also explore how stress in spoken English can help distinguish between different meanings.

The lesson then examines how compound nouns are made plural. Students learn to identify the most important element of the compound and practise examples including footballs, sheep dips, fathers-in-law, platefuls, cryptocurrencies and eyeliners.

Finally, students create their own compound nouns and complete a series of word and picture challenges involving familiar compounds such as snowman, armchair, teapot, starfish, bathroom, paintbrush, sandcastle, crossroads, moonlight, butterfly, popcorn, dragonfly, raincoat, sunflower, bookshelf and seesaw.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to recognise and use Standard English more accurately, correct common non-standard constructions, understand how compound nouns are formed and spelled, and confidently identify, create and pluralise a range of compound words.

lessons.title: Autumn Starter
lessons.description:
In this Autumn Starter lesson, students revise a range of English skills through grammar, comprehension, spelling, punctuation and writing activities.

This lesson includes:
✔ Using standard verb forms correctly
✔ Mixed comprehension and prediction skills
✔ Practising statutory spelling words
✔ Using apostrophes for plural possession
✔ Fronted adverbials and prepositions
✔ Correctly punctuating direct speech
✔ Using subordinating conjunctions

Students begin by identifying incorrect verb forms and correcting sentences using standard English, including choosing accurately between forms such as did and done, saw and seen, and was and were.

The reading activity follows Rishabh as he discovers an old book called The Mystery of the Moon. Students retrieve information, use contextual clues, identify vocabulary and make predictions based on evidence from the text.

Students then practise statutory spelling words including breath, library, remember, arrive, potatoes, special and through, using selected letters to reveal the hidden word harvest.

The punctuation section focuses on apostrophes for plural possession. Students identify where apostrophes belong in examples such as the squirrels’ acorns, the badgers’ set, the trees’ berries, the foxes’ digging and the moles’ hills.

Finally, students apply a mixture of punctuation, grammar and vocabulary skills to picture-based writing. They construct sentences containing a fronted adverbial, a preposition, correctly punctuated direct speech and a subordinating conjunction.

By the end of the lesson, students will have revised and applied a broad range of Year 4 English skills involving grammar, reading comprehension, spelling, punctuation and sentence construction.

lessons.title: Prepositions, Adverbial Phrases
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of prepositions and adverbial phrases. They learn how prepositions describe place, time and movement, identify prepositions within sentences and passages, and distinguish between prepositions and subordinating conjunctions. Students then explore how adverbial phrases add information about how, when, where, why and for how long an action happens.

This lesson includes:
✔ Identifying prepositions of place, time and movement
✔ Using prepositions accurately in sentences
✔ Distinguishing prepositions from other word classes
✔ Recognising when words such as after and since act as prepositions or subordinating conjunctions
✔ Identifying and using adverbial phrases

Students begin by exploring what prepositions are and how they describe relationships involving place, time and movement.

Students will:
✔ Identify common prepositions
✔ Describe the position of objects using prepositions
✔ Sort prepositions from other word classes
✔ Recognise prepositional phrases
✔ Use appropriate prepositions to complete sentences

Students then apply their understanding by creating sentences from pictures and identifying prepositions within longer passages.

Students will:
✔ Use prepositions of location accurately
✔ Use prepositions of time accurately
✔ Use prepositions of movement and direction
✔ Replace prepositions while maintaining grammatical sentences
✔ Explain how changing a preposition changes meaning

The lesson also explores words that can function as either prepositions or subordinating conjunctions depending on their grammatical context.

Students will:
✔ Examine words such as after, before, until, as and since
✔ Identify whether a word introduces a noun phrase or a subordinate clause
✔ Distinguish prepositions from subordinating conjunctions
✔ Use surrounding sentence structure to determine grammatical function

The lesson then introduces adverbial phrases and explores the additional information they provide within sentences.

Students will:
✔ Identify adverbial phrases in sentences
✔ Recognise adverbials describing how an action happens
✔ Identify adverbials of time and frequency
✔ Recognise adverbials describing place
✔ Identify phrases explaining why or for how long something happens

Students practise identifying examples such as 'in a rush', 'at once', 'every day', 'this morning', 'since Wednesday', 'almost always', 'with a limp', 'like a snake', 'one by one' and 'in a line'.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently identify and use prepositions of place, time and movement, distinguish prepositions from subordinating conjunctions, and recognise how adverbial phrases provide additional information about actions and events.

lessons.title: Present perfect tense
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of the present perfect tense and learn how it differs from the simple past tense. They explore how the present perfect connects actions or events from the past to the present and practise forming it correctly using has or have with the past participle of a verb.

This lesson includes:
✔ Recognising the present perfect tense
✔ Distinguishing between simple past and present perfect tense
✔ Using has and have correctly
✔ Understanding past participles
✔ Converting past tense sentences into the present perfect
✔ Identifying regular and irregular verb forms
✔ Choosing the correct tense according to context and meaning
✔ Using present perfect forms accurately in sentences

Students begin by learning how sentences can be changed from the past tense into the present perfect tense using has or have with the appropriate verb form. They explore examples such as 'the alien won' becoming 'the alien has won' and 'the aliens landed' becoming 'the aliens have landed'.

Students also learn that the present perfect can describe something that began in the past and is still continuing in the present. For example, 'Timmy has been in his spaceship for twenty years' tells us that Timmy entered the spaceship in the past and remains there now.

Students will:
✔ Convert past tense verbs into present perfect forms
✔ Use have with I, you, we and they
✔ Use has with he, she and it
✔ Recognise common irregular forms such as grown, done, eaten, broken, gone, fallen and seen
✔ Create their own past tense and present perfect sentences

The lesson provides extensive practice with regular and irregular verbs. Students compare forms such as ate and have eaten, broke and has broken, went and have gone, fell and have fallen, and saw and have seen.

Students then compare sentences in the simple past and present perfect tenses and learn how timing affects which form should be used. The simple past is used for actions or events that started and finished in the past, whereas the present perfect is used when an earlier action is still true, continues into the present or has an effect on what is happening now.

Further activities involve matching past tense sentences with their present perfect equivalents, rewriting a football match recount in the present perfect tense, identifying the tense used in sentences and selecting the most appropriate verb form according to context.

Students also learn that the present perfect uses the auxiliary verb have or has followed by the past participle, or third form, of the main verb. They practise choosing accurate forms such as has grown rather than has grew, have done rather than have did, has come rather than has came, and have forgotten rather than have forgot.

By the end of the lesson, students will confidently distinguish between the simple past and present perfect tenses, use has and have correctly, select appropriate past participles and understand when a past action remains connected to the present.

lessons.title: Prefixes
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of prefixes and how adding a prefix to the beginning of a root word can create a new word and change its meaning. The lesson focuses particularly on the prefixes super, auto and anti. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding what a prefix is
✔ Exploring the meanings of super, auto and anti
✔ Using prefixes to create new words
✔ Using word meanings to identify the correct prefix
✔ Working out the meanings of unfamiliar prefixed words
✔ Matching prefixes with appropriate root words
✔ Using prefixed words accurately in sentences
✔ Applying grammar and punctuation skills in a short writing task

Students begin by learning that a prefix is a group of letters added to the beginning of a word to create a new word. They explore examples such as supermarket, autograph and antifreeze.

Students then investigate the meanings of three important prefixes:
✔ super – meaning greater, more than or above
✔ auto – meaning self or own
✔ anti – meaning against or the opposite of :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

Students use these meanings to explore words such as supernatural, superhero, supernova, automatic, autograph, autobiography, antifreeze, antibiotic and antiseptic.

They then apply their knowledge to unfamiliar vocabulary, using prefixes as clues to work out word meanings. Activities include identifying words such as superpower, autopilot and antisocial, and selecting the correct prefix to create words such as autocue, antidote and superglue.

Students will:
✔ Choose an appropriate prefix for a root word
✔ Explain the meaning of the new word
✔ Use the new word in a sentence
✔ Match prefixes to root words to form recognised English words
✔ Distinguish between possible prefix choices according to meaning and context

Further practice includes creating and using words such as automobile, antiseptic, superstore, antiviral, superfood, antibacterial, superstar, antibiotic, anticlimax and supersonic.

Students also complete quizzes in which they select the correct prefixed word and add super, auto or anti to words within sentences to make the meaning correct.

The lesson finishes with a creative writing activity called 'Stairway to the Unknown'. Students write five sentences inspired by a photograph, including a prepositional phrase, the personal pronoun he, a possessive apostrophe, an adverb and a question sentence. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}

By the end of the lesson, students will confidently understand and use the prefixes super, auto and anti, use prefixes to build new words, and use their knowledge of prefixes to work out the meanings of unfamiliar vocabulary.

lessons.title: Estimate, Compare & Calculate Money
lessons.description:
Today’s lesson lays the foundation for working with money in the real world.

In this video, students will learn how to estimate with money.
We will explore how to round amounts to the nearest pound, use number lines to check, and decide when to round up or down.
Students will practise adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing money in real-life shopping situations, and finding change quickly and accurately.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to:
✔ Estimate totals confidently
✔ Round prices to make calculations easier
✔ Work out exact costs and share amounts fairly
✔ Use quick methods to calculate change

This lesson builds strong money skills, boosts confidence with mental maths, and prepares students for everyday problem-solving.

lessons.title: Subtraction
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to subtract four-digit numbers using the column method.
They start with simple calculations and move on to exchanges.

This lesson includes:
✔ Subtraction with and without exchanges
✔ Place value models for understanding
✔ Fun puzzles and challenges
✔ Real-life examples
✔ Efficient subtraction strategies

By the end of the lesson, learners will be confident with column subtraction.

lessons.title: Addition and Subtraction
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students explore addition and subtraction problem-solving using real-life examples.
They learn how to choose the correct operation and check answers using the inverse.

This lesson includes:
✔ Two-step word problems
✔ Addition and subtraction keyword activities
✔ Real-life examples
✔ Checking answers using inverse operations
✔ Practice challenges
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Area
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students explore the concept of area.
They learn how to measure the space inside shapes using unit squares and multiplication.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding area in real life
✔ Counting squares to find area
✔ Using multiplication for rectangles
✔ Working with half-squares and composite shapes
✔ Practice activities
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Rule of 3
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn the Rule of Three to solve proportion problems.
They practise cross multiplication and division using real-life examples.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding proportions
✔ Step-by-step Rule of Three method
✔ Real-life word problems
✔ Measurement conversions
✔ Practice worksheets
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Converting Lengths
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to convert between different units of length.
They practise converting and comparing measurements.

This lesson includes:
✔ Ordering units of length
✔ Converting between mm, cm, m, and km
✔ Real-life examples
✔ Solving word problems
✔ Comparing and ordering measurements
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Comparing and Calculating Lengths
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to compare and order lengths.
They convert between centimetres, metres, and kilometres to solve problems.

This lesson includes:
✔ Converting units of length
✔ Comparing and ordering measurements
✔ Real-life word problems
✔ Fun comparison challenges
✔ Subtraction problems with distances
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Fractions 1
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students build a strong understanding of fractions.
They explore wholes, equal parts, and fractions greater than one using models and number lines.

This lesson includes:
✔ Identifying wholes and equal parts
✔ Unit and non-unit fractions
✔ Completing fractions to make a whole
✔ Counting in fractions on number lines
✔ Improper fractions and mixed numbers
✔ Step-by-step practice questions
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Fractions 2
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn about mixed numbers and how to represent, compare, and order fractions.
They use number lines and visual models to build confidence.

This lesson includes:
✔ Counting in fractional steps
✔ Writing mixed numbers from models
✔ Placing fractions on number lines
✔ Comparing and ordering mixed numbers
✔ Practice activities
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Number and Place Value 1
lessons.description:
In this video, students will learn how numbers build up to 1000 and beyond.
We will use visual models and place value charts to explore thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones.

Students will also:
✔ Represent thousands using visual models
✔ Partition numbers in standard and non-standard ways
✔ Break 1000 into equal parts
✔ Compare, order, and compose four-digit numbers
✔ Solve word problems using partitioning

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently represent and partition large numbers.
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Fractions 3
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students explore improper fractions and mixed numbers.
They learn how to recognise, represent, and convert between them.

This lesson includes:
✔ Identifying improper fractions
✔ Using visual models and number lines
✔ Converting mixed numbers and improper fractions
✔ Times-table reasoning
✔ Guided practice and challenges
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Fractions 4
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to add and subtract fractions with the same denominator.
They also work with mixed numbers and improper fractions.

This lesson includes:
✔ Adding fractions with the same denominator
✔ Using models to visualise calculations
✔ Adding fractions to mixed numbers
✔ Subtracting fractions and mixed numbers
✔ Converting improper fractions to mixed numbers
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Fractions 5
lessons.description: Fractions 5: decimals, tenths, hundredths and partitioning.
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Fractions 6
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students explore decimal halves and quarters.
They learn about equivalent fractions and rounding decimals.

This lesson includes:
✔ Equivalent fractions for halves and quarters
✔ Writing halves and quarters as decimals
✔ Using models and number lines
✔ Rounding decimals to the nearest whole
✔ Applying place value reasoning
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Fractions 7
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students compare and order decimal numbers.
They use place value knowledge and number lines to decide which decimals are greater or smaller.

This lesson includes:
✔ Linking fractions to decimals
✔ Comparing decimals using place value
✔ Using greater than, less than, and equals symbols
✔ Ordering decimals in ascending and descending order
✔ Solving mixed comparison problems
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Time 1
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn about years, months, weeks and days, and how these units of time are connected. They practise naming and ordering the months of the year, recalling how many days are in each month, identifying leap years, and converting between years and months. They also learn to use calendars to answer date questions and convert between weeks and days in real-life contexts.

This lesson includes:
✔ Ordering months and recalling the number of days in each month
✔ Understanding years, months, calendars, weeks and days
✔ Identifying leap years and explaining why February can have 29 days
✔ Converting between years and months
✔ Converting between weeks and days
✔ Solving mixed-unit problems with years and months or weeks and days
✔ Reading calendars to find dates and days of the week
✔ Using times tables and division facts to solve time problems
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Time 2
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn to convert between hours and minutes, and between minutes and seconds. They use the fact that there are 60 minutes in one hour and 60 seconds in one minute to solve conversions, compare durations, and work out mixed-unit time problems. They also apply these skills to real-life reasoning questions involving schedules, reading challenges and elapsed time.

This lesson includes:
✔ Converting hours to minutes and minutes to hours
✔ Converting minutes to seconds and seconds to minutes
✔ Solving mixed-unit problems such as hours and minutes, or minutes and seconds
✔ Comparing durations using greater than, less than and equals
✔ Using multiplication and division facts with 60
✔ Solving elapsed-time problems in real-life contexts
✔ Ordering times from shortest to longest
✔ Interpreting and solving reasoning problems with time tables and totals
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Time 3
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to convert between analogue clocks and twelve-hour digital times, and how to interpret and use the 24-hour clock. They practise reading minutes past and minutes to the hour, using a.m. and p.m. correctly, and converting times between 12-hour and 24-hour formats. They also solve elapsed-time problems involving start times and finish times.

This lesson includes:
✔ Reading analogue clocks and matching them to digital times
✔ Understanding minutes past and minutes to the hour
✔ Using a.m. and p.m. correctly
✔ Converting analogue times to 12-hour digital times
✔ Converting 12-hour times to 24-hour clock times
✔ Knowing when to add 12 for p.m. times after noon
✔ Solving start-time and finish-time problems
✔ Explaining and correcting common mistakes in time conversion
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Time 4
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to convert from 24-hour clock to 12-hour digital and analogue times. They practise identifying whether a 24-hour time is a.m. or p.m., subtracting 12 from times after noon, and matching 24-hour times to correct analogue clock faces. They also solve reasoning problems involving equivalent times and common conversion errors.

This lesson includes:
✔ Converting from 24-hour clock to 12-hour digital times
✔ Identifying whether a 24-hour time is a.m. or p.m.
✔ Subtracting 12 from times after 12:59 to convert to p.m. times
✔ Matching 24-hour times to analogue clocks
✔ Converting activities and schedules between time formats
✔ Explaining common mistakes in 24-hour to 12-hour conversion
✔ Recognising equivalent analogue, 12-hour and 24-hour times
✔ Solving reasoning problems using different clock representations
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Statistics 1
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students are introduced to statistics and learn how to collect, interpret and present discrete data.

In this video, students will learn what discrete data is.
They will understand that discrete data is counted and cannot have in-between values, such as the number of cars or children.

Students will begin with a real-life investigation, analysing different coloured cars passing a school. They will:
✔ Identify the most common category
✔ Compare values between categories
✔ Calculate totals

The lesson then introduces pictograms.
Students will learn that pictograms use symbols to represent data and that a key is essential.

Students will also:
✔ Interpret pictograms using a key
✔ Work out totals from symbols
✔ Compare categories
✔ Understand that symbols can represent more than one unit
✔ Use parts of symbols for smaller values

Next, students will learn how to draw pictograms.
They will:
✔ Choose an appropriate key
✔ Represent data accurately
✔ Use fractions of symbols where needed

The lesson then introduces bar charts.
Students will learn that bar charts:
✔ Have a horizontal axis for categories
✔ Have a vertical axis for values
✔ Use a number scale
✔ Include titles and labelled axes
✔ Have equal-width bars with gaps

Students will also:
✔ Read values from scales
✔ Compare categories
✔ Calculate differences and totals
✔ Choose appropriate scales such as 1, 2, 5 or 10

The lesson then extends to more advanced bar charts.

Grouped bar charts:
✔ Compare subcategories such as boys and girls
✔ Use multiple bars per category
✔ Require a key or legend

Stacked bar charts:
✔ Combine subcategories into one bar
✔ Help compare totals and parts together

Students will apply their learning to real datasets, such as birthdays across months.
They will interpret data, compare values, and answer questions.

The lesson then introduces Venn diagrams.
Students will learn that:
✔ Each circle represents a set
✔ Overlapping sections show shared data
✔ Items in overlaps belong to multiple categories

Students will also interpret Venn diagrams by:
✔ Identifying where data belongs
✔ Answering questions about combinations
✔ Understanding multiple overlaps with three sets

Finally, students are introduced to Carroll diagrams as another way to organise data into categories.

By the end of the lesson, learners will understand how to present and interpret data using different methods and use this knowledge to answer comparison and total-based questions.
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Number and Place Value 2
lessons.description:
In this video, students will build on their knowledge of partitioning and place value.
They will represent and break apart four-digit numbers and write them in expanded form.

Students will also:
✔ Partition four-digit numbers using place value models
✔ Solve word problems using partitioning
✔ Explore number lines and currency examples
✔ Find 1000 more or 1000 less
✔ Play games to apply these skills

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently represent and manipulate four-digit numbers.
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Statistics 2
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students build on their understanding of statistics by interpreting and drawing bar charts and time graphs using both discrete and continuous data.

Students begin by using timelines and bar charts to investigate kings and queens from history.
They will:
✔ Read timelines accurately
✔ Match years to positions on a scale
✔ Interpret bar charts
✔ Compare lengths of reigns
✔ Calculate totals and differences from charts

The lesson then introduces grouped bar charts.
Students learn that grouped bar charts compare two sets of related data using a key or legend.

Students will also:
✔ Compare two pieces of information side by side
✔ Interpret grouped bar charts
✔ Identify similarities and differences in data
✔ Answer reasoning questions using scales and bars

Next, students explore countryside statistics using tally charts and frequency tables.
They will:
✔ Count tally marks in groups of five
✔ Complete missing frequencies
✔ Interpret discrete data
✔ Calculate totals and differences
✔ Identify the highest and lowest frequencies

Students then move on to drawing and interpreting bar charts.
They learn that bar charts:
✔ Use horizontal and vertical axes
✔ Need a suitable scale
✔ Must include labels and titles
✔ Require equal-width bars with gaps between them

Students will also:
✔ Spot mistakes in incorrect bar charts
✔ Compare categories visually
✔ Solve reasoning problems using data
✔ Interpret scales accurately

The lesson then introduces continuous data and time graphs.
Students learn that continuous data is measured and can have in-between values.

Students will:
✔ Understand the difference between discrete and continuous data
✔ Read and interpret time graphs
✔ Measure distance against time
✔ Estimate values between plotted points
✔ Calculate changes over time

Students also learn how to:
✔ Read scales carefully
✔ Follow points across axes
✔ Find approximate values from graphs
✔ Compare distances and times

The lesson then explores true and false reasoning questions using bar charts.
Students will:
✔ Evaluate statements using data
✔ Calculate totals and differences
✔ Explain whether statements are true or false

Next, students investigate temperatures using thermometers, bar charts and time graphs.
They will:
✔ Read temperatures in degrees Celsius
✔ Record continuous data
✔ Compare temperatures across days
✔ Calculate temperature differences
✔ Decide which graph type is most appropriate

Students then compare temperatures from different cities around the world.
They will:
✔ Interpret bar charts showing city temperatures
✔ Compare values between cities
✔ Identify equal and greater values
✔ Answer multi-step comparison questions

Finally, students are introduced to double time graphs.
They learn that double time graphs compare two sets of continuous data over the same time period.

Students will also:
✔ Compare two lines on one graph
✔ Calculate differences between datasets
✔ Interpret changes over time visually
✔ Analyse patterns and trends

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently interpret and compare data using timelines, tally charts, grouped bar charts, bar charts, time graphs and double time graphs.
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Statistics 3
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students continue developing their statistics skills by interpreting and drawing bar charts, line graphs and time graphs using real-life data.

Students begin with gardening statistics.
They measure sunflower heights using a metre stick and record the data in a table.

Students will:
✔ Read scales accurately
✔ Measure heights in centimetres
✔ Complete data tables
✔ Compare values
✔ Calculate differences and totals

The lesson then explores which type of graph is most suitable for presenting data.
Students learn that:
✔ Bar charts are useful for comparing categories
✔ Time graphs are used when data changes over time
✔ Discrete data uses separate categories
✔ Continuous data is measured over time

Students then interpret bar charts by:
✔ Identifying the tallest and shortest values
✔ Calculating differences between categories
✔ Finding combined totals
✔ Solving reasoning questions using graph data

Next, students investigate runner bean growth over two weeks.
They learn how to present continuous data using a time graph.

Students will also:
✔ Understand how time graphs show change over time
✔ Read horizontal and vertical axes
✔ Choose suitable scales
✔ Plot and join points correctly
✔ Interpret approximate values between points

Students practise answering questions from time graphs by:
✔ Reading measurements accurately
✔ Calculating growth over time
✔ Estimating values from graph lines
✔ Identifying when measurements reach certain values

The lesson then introduces double time graphs.
Students learn that double time graphs compare two sets of data measured over the same period of time.

Students will:
✔ Compare two lines on one graph
✔ Read values from different datasets
✔ Calculate differences between lines
✔ Analyse changes over time visually

Next, students explore sponsored swim statistics.
They identify mistakes in bar charts and learn how incorrect data presentation can affect interpretation.

Students will also:
✔ Spot incorrect bar heights
✔ Compare chart data with frequency tables
✔ Correct graph errors
✔ Interpret swimming competition data
✔ Solve reasoning problems using bar charts

The lesson then introduces line graphs for journeys and distance over time.
Students learn that line graphs can be used to show continuous movement and changing measurements.

Students will:
✔ Estimate distances and times from line graphs
✔ Read approximate values
✔ Calculate time differences
✔ Interpret journeys visually

Finally, students investigate pets statistics.
They interpret bar charts and line graphs involving pet ownership, animal weights and kitten growth.

Students will also:
✔ Compare quantities from bar charts
✔ Calculate totals and differences
✔ Read decimal values from graphs
✔ Interpret weight graphs over time
✔ Estimate values between plotted points

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently interpret, compare and analyse data using bar charts, line graphs, time graphs and double time graphs.
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Multiplication and Division
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their multiplication and division skills by exploring multiples of 3, multiplying and dividing by 6, and multiplying and dividing by 9.

Students begin by learning the three times table using groups, repeated addition and number lines.

Students will:
✔ Count in multiples of 3
✔ Use repeated addition to represent multiplication
✔ Link groups of objects to multiplication calculations
✔ Recognise patterns in the three times table
✔ Use number lines to calculate multiples of 3

The lesson then explores how known multiplication facts can help solve larger calculations.
Students learn to build on known facts such as twelve times three to calculate more challenging multiples.

Students will also:
✔ Use known facts to solve larger calculations
✔ Count on in equal groups
✔ Explain multiplication patterns
✔ Apply efficient mental maths strategies

Next, students investigate multiples of 3 using digit sums.
They learn that if the sum of the digits is a multiple of 3, then the whole number is also a multiple of 3.

Students will:
✔ Find digit sums
✔ Test whether numbers are multiples of 3
✔ Identify multiples in large numbers
✔ Use divisibility rules confidently

The lesson then moves on to multiplying and dividing by 6.
Students use groups, sharing, grouping and arrays to explore multiplication and division facts.

Students will also:
✔ Represent multiplication using equal groups
✔ Use arrays to show rows and columns
✔ Understand that multiplication is commutative
✔ Divide by sharing equally
✔ Divide by grouping
✔ Write multiplication and division calculations from arrays

Students then explore fact families.
They learn how multiplication and division facts are linked together.

Students will:
✔ Create multiplication and division fact families
✔ Use arrays to identify related facts
✔ Correct mistakes in fact families
✔ Understand the relationship between multiplication and division

The lesson also shows how the six times table links to the three times table.
Students learn that multiplying by 6 can be found by doubling the answers in the three times table.

Students practise:
✔ Doubling multiples of 3
✔ Building fluency in the six times table
✔ Splitting numbers to solve larger multiplications
✔ Using partitioning strategies

Next, students move on to multiplying and dividing by 9.
They explore equal groups, arrays and fact families involving multiples of 9.

Students will also:
✔ Count in multiples of 9
✔ Use repeated addition with groups of 9
✔ Represent multiplication using arrays
✔ Solve division calculations by grouping
✔ Create fact families for the nine times table

Finally, students learn efficient strategies for calculating larger multiples of 9.
They use partitioning and known facts such as ten times nine to solve more challenging calculations.

Students will:
✔ Split numbers into easier parts
✔ Use known multiplication facts
✔ Add and subtract multiples efficiently
✔ Solve larger multiplication calculations mentally

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently identify multiples of 3 and use multiplication and division facts for 6 and 9 to solve a wide range of calculations.
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Shapes 1
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of angles and polygons. They learn how to identify, compare and order different types of angles and recognise angles within shapes.

Students begin by revising clockwise and anticlockwise turns.
They learn to identify quarter turns, half turns and three-quarter turns in different directions.

Students will:
✔ Identify clockwise and anticlockwise turns
✔ Recognise quarter, half and three-quarter turns
✔ Describe turns using correct mathematical language
✔ Find more than one way to reach the same position

The lesson then introduces angles as a measure of turn.
Students learn that an angle is formed between two straight lines and that a larger turn creates a larger angle.

Students will also:
✔ Understand angles as measures of turn
✔ Relate quarter turns to right angles
✔ Recognise that a full turn equals four right angles
✔ Identify right angles in different orientations

Next, students explore acute angles.
They learn that acute angles are smaller than a right angle.

Students will:
✔ Identify acute angles in different positions
✔ Compare acute angles
✔ Decide whether statements about acute angles are true or false
✔ Understand that acute angles can be different sizes

The lesson then introduces obtuse angles.
Students learn that obtuse angles are larger than a right angle but smaller than a half turn.

Students will also:
✔ Identify obtuse angles
✔ Compare obtuse and acute angles
✔ Use right-angle checkers to classify angles
✔ Explain reasoning using mathematical vocabulary

Students then investigate combinations of angles.
They learn that two acute angles can sometimes combine to make an obtuse angle, depending on their sizes.

Students will:
✔ Classify angles accurately
✔ Explain whether statements are always, sometimes or never true
✔ Compare different angle sizes
✔ Apply logical reasoning to angle problems

The lesson then explores polygons and interior angles.
Students learn that polygons are two-dimensional shapes with straight sides and that the angles inside them are called interior angles.

Students will also:
✔ Identify interior angles in polygons
✔ Count acute and obtuse angles within shapes
✔ Recognise different angle types in triangles, quadrilaterals and other polygons
✔ Correct misconceptions about polygon angles

Students then use a Venn diagram to classify polygons according to their interior angles.

They will:
✔ Sort polygons with acute angles
✔ Sort polygons with obtuse angles
✔ Identify polygons containing both acute and obtuse angles
✔ Compare different polygon properties

The lesson then focuses on comparing and ordering angles.
Students learn that the greater the turn, the greater the angle.

Students will also:
✔ Compare acute angles by size
✔ Compare obtuse angles by size
✔ Understand that larger acute angles are closer to a right angle
✔ Understand that larger obtuse angles are closer to a straight angle

Finally, students learn that the size of an angle depends on the amount of turn, not the length of the lines forming the angle.

Students will:
✔ Compare angles accurately regardless of line length
✔ Recognise equal angles in different drawings
✔ Explain why longer lines do not create larger angles
✔ Apply angle reasoning to solve comparison problems

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently identify, classify, compare and order acute, obtuse and right angles, and recognise how angles are used within polygons.
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Shapes 2
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of triangles and quadrilaterals. They learn how to identify, classify and compare different types of triangles and quadrilaterals using their properties.

Students begin by revising common polygons and identifying which shapes are triangles.
They learn that a triangle is a closed two-dimensional shape with three straight sides.

Students will:
✔ Identify common polygons
✔ Recognise triangles in different orientations
✔ Explain why some shapes are not triangles
✔ Use the properties of sides and vertices to classify shapes

The lesson then introduces different types of triangles.
Students learn how to identify equilateral, isosceles, scalene and right-angled triangles.

Students will also:
✔ Recognise equilateral triangles with three equal sides and three equal angles
✔ Identify isosceles triangles with two equal sides and two equal angles
✔ Identify scalene triangles with no equal sides
✔ Recognise right-angled triangles using the right-angle symbol
✔ Sort triangles according to their properties

Next, students explore perimeter problems involving triangles.
They use equal-side markings and known lengths to calculate missing sides and total perimeters.

Students will:
✔ Calculate the perimeter of equilateral triangles
✔ Calculate the perimeter of isosceles triangles
✔ Find missing side lengths using equal-side markings
✔ Use addition, subtraction and division to solve perimeter problems
✔ Apply reasoning skills to multi-step triangle questions

The lesson then uses clues to identify different triangle types.

Students will also:
✔ Match properties to triangle names
✔ Explain their reasoning using mathematical vocabulary
✔ Identify triangles from side and angle clues
✔ Compare different triangle classifications

The lesson then introduces parallel lines and quadrilaterals.
Students learn how to identify parallel sides and classify shapes according to their properties.

Students will:
✔ Identify pairs of parallel lines in polygons
✔ Understand that parallel lines never meet
✔ Recognise quadrilaterals as four-sided polygons
✔ Identify vertices and sides of quadrilaterals
✔ Distinguish between regular and irregular quadrilaterals

Students then compare different quadrilaterals.
They explore squares, rectangles, parallelograms, rhombuses, kites and trapeziums.

Students will also:
✔ Identify properties of squares and rectangles
✔ Compare parallelograms and rhombuses
✔ Recognise the properties of kites
✔ Identify trapeziums using parallel sides
✔ Understand which properties are shared between quadrilaterals

The lesson also develops reasoning skills using sorting and classification activities.

Students will:
✔ Sort quadrilaterals using properties such as right angles, equal sides and parallel sides
✔ Identify and correct classification mistakes
✔ Explain why shapes remain the same when rotated
✔ Use clues to identify quadrilaterals
✔ Apply mathematical vocabulary accurately

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently identify and classify triangles and quadrilaterals, calculate triangle perimeters, and use shape properties to solve reasoning and classification problems.
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Shapes 3
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of regular polygons, lines of symmetry and reflective symmetry. They learn how to identify symmetrical shapes, count lines of symmetry and complete symmetrical figures accurately.

Students begin by exploring regular and irregular polygons.
They learn that regular polygons have sides of equal length and angles of equal size.

Students will:
✔ Identify regular and irregular polygons
✔ Recognise pentagons, hexagons, heptagons and octagons
✔ Classify polygons by the number of sides
✔ Explain the difference between regular and irregular shapes

The lesson then explores perimeter in regular polygons.
Students learn that knowing the length of one side is enough to calculate the perimeter of a regular polygon.

Students will also:
✔ Calculate perimeters using multiplication
✔ Use equal side lengths to solve perimeter problems
✔ Apply division to find side lengths from known perimeters
✔ Solve reasoning problems involving regular polygons

Next, students investigate how perimeter and side length are connected.
They explore which regular polygons can be created from a fixed length of ribbon.

Students will:
✔ Divide perimeters into equal side lengths
✔ Identify when side lengths are whole numbers
✔ Compare different regular polygons
✔ Use multiplication and division to justify answers

The lesson then introduces lines of symmetry.
Students learn that a line of symmetry divides a shape into two matching mirror-image halves.

Students will also:
✔ Identify vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines of symmetry
✔ Use mirrors to test symmetry
✔ Explain why some lines are not lines of symmetry
✔ Recognise symmetry in different orientations

Students then explore lines of symmetry in common shapes.

Students will:
✔ Identify lines of symmetry in squares, rectangles and triangles
✔ Recognise shapes with no lines of symmetry
✔ Understand that circles have infinitely many lines of symmetry
✔ Compare the symmetry of different polygons

The lesson also investigates symmetry in regular polygons.
Students discover patterns between the number of sides and the number of lines of symmetry.

Students will:
✔ Count lines of symmetry in regular polygons
✔ Identify patterns in regular shapes
✔ Compare polygons with the most and fewest lines of symmetry
✔ Explain mathematical relationships using evidence

Next, students explore symmetrical figures.
They learn how lines of symmetry create matching mirror-image halves.

Students will also:
✔ Identify lines of symmetry in everyday objects and images
✔ Recognise symmetrical figures in different orientations
✔ Explain why figures are symmetrical
✔ Compare different types of symmetry

The lesson then develops reflection skills using grids.
Students learn how to reflect patterns accurately across mirror lines.

Students will:
✔ Reflect shaded squares across vertical and horizontal mirror lines
✔ Measure distances from the mirror line
✔ Complete symmetrical patterns
✔ Check reflections for accuracy

Students then apply reflection techniques to polygons.

They will:
✔ Identify and reflect vertices accurately
✔ Construct reflected polygons using grid coordinates
✔ Complete dissected symmetrical polygons
✔ Identify the polygons formed after reflection
✔ Solve reasoning problems involving vertices and symmetry

Finally, students explore reflections across more than one line of symmetry.
They learn how repeated reflections create fully symmetrical patterns.

Students will:
✔ Reflect shapes across multiple mirror lines
✔ Complete symmetrical designs in all directions
✔ Check that reflected points remain equal distances from mirror lines
✔ Apply symmetry skills to increasingly complex figures

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently identify regular polygons, calculate their perimeters, recognise and count lines of symmetry, and complete symmetrical patterns and reflected shapes accurately.

lessons.title: Compare and Contrast Text
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to compare and contrast texts by identifying similarities and differences, organising information using Venn diagrams and using appropriate signal words to explain comparisons clearly.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding the difference between comparing and contrasting
✔ Identifying similarities and differences between texts and ideas
✔ Organising information using two-way and three-way Venn diagrams
✔ Using compare signal words such as also, similarly, both and likewise
✔ Using contrast signal words such as although, however, unlike and in contrast
✔ Comparing information about Easter and Eid Al-Fitr
✔ Understanding the purpose of religious festivals
✔ Exploring similarities and differences in religious celebrations
✔ Comparing periods of fasting, reflection and self-discipline
✔ Identifying how festivals involve family, worship, food and gifts
✔ Understanding comparative and superlative forms
✔ Choosing appropriate comparative and superlative words in context

Students begin by learning that to compare means to identify things that are the same or similar, while to contrast means to identify differences. They explore how taking notes and organising information in a Venn diagram can make relationships between texts easier to understand.

The lesson introduces both two-way and three-way Venn diagrams. Students learn that separate sections represent differences while overlapping sections show characteristics or information that two or more subjects have in common.

Students then develop the language needed to communicate comparisons effectively. Compare signal words include also, similarly, as well as, the same as, both, too, in addition and likewise. Contrast signal words include although, differ, even though, however, in contrast, unlike and on the other hand.

Students apply these skills by comparing Easter and Eid Al-Fitr. They explore the religious significance of each festival and consider similarities such as gathering with family and friends, attending places of worship, sharing special meals and celebrating important aspects of faith.

The lesson also examines how the dates of both festivals can change from year to year and how their timing is connected with lunar cycles. Students compare Ramadan before Eid Al-Fitr with Lent before Easter and explore how fasting, self-discipline, prayer and reflection can form part of religious observance before a period of celebration.

Students consider further similarities in the celebrations themselves, including feasting with family and friends and exchanging gifts. They examine traditions such as Eid gifts and Easter eggs and consider the significance attached to these practices.

The final section develops students' understanding of comparative and superlative language. Students choose between forms such as smaller and smallest, faster and fastest, further and furthest, worse and worst, less and least, better and best, and more and most according to whether two things or a wider group are being compared.

By the end of the lesson, students will be able to identify and organise similarities and differences, use appropriate compare and contrast vocabulary, apply these skills to information from different sources and distinguish accurately between comparative and superlative forms.

lessons.title: Advertising
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students explore how advertising works, why advertisements are created and the persuasive techniques advertisers use to influence what people think, feel and choose.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding the purpose of advertising
✔ Identifying different forms of advertising and media
✔ Understanding consumers and target audiences
✔ Exploring how adverts use emotions to influence people
✔ Recognising persuasive advertising techniques
✔ Identifying slogans, jingles, logos and special offers
✔ Understanding celebrity endorsement and brand ambassadors
✔ Exploring hidden advertising and product placement
✔ Recognising bias, misinformation, fake news and propaganda
✔ Understanding advertising guidelines and responsible advertising
✔ Identifying persuasive and appealing language
✔ Recognising strong claims and promises in adverts
✔ Using questions, humour, alliteration, rhyme and word play
✔ Analysing how words, pictures and colours work together in adverts
✔ Exploring how food advertising influences consumer choices
✔ Recognising marketing strategies such as freebies, bargains and colourful packaging
✔ Considering the influence of celebrities and cartoon characters
✔ Thinking critically about healthy and unhealthy food advertising

Students begin by exploring the different advertisements they encounter through television, newspapers, radio, the Internet, social media and other forms of media. They learn that advertising is designed to communicate messages and often aims to persuade consumers to buy or use a product or service.

The lesson examines how advertisers identify particular target audiences and carefully choose words, images, colours, sounds and emotions to make products appear attractive. Students explore techniques including catchy slogans and jingles, logos, celebrity endorsements, special offers, product placement and hidden advertising.

Students also develop their media literacy by considering bias and misinformation. They learn about fake news and propaganda and discuss why information presented through media should be examined critically rather than automatically accepted as true.

The lesson then focuses on persuasive writing. Students investigate appealing language such as free, exclusive, new and improved and special offer, as well as strong promises designed to make products seem irresistible. They explore how questions, humour, positive reviews, alliteration, rhyme and word play can make advertising memorable.

Students analyse an example advertisement for Billy's Big Burger, identifying its catchy title, rhetorical question, appealing language, alliteration, strong claims and sensory language. They consider how these features work together to persuade the reader.

The lesson then explores advertising and food choices in greater depth. Students investigate strategies including celebrity endorsement, cartoon characters, catchy jingles, freebies, colourful packaging, slogans, logos, lifestyle imagery and bargains. They consider how these techniques can influence consumers, particularly children, sometimes without them realising it.

Finally, students think critically about advertising unhealthy foods and consider whether an attractive advert necessarily represents a healthy or sensible choice. They compare food advertisements, investigate persuasive strategies and consider how advertising can affect their own decisions.

By the end of the lesson, students will be able to recognise and explain a wide range of advertising and persuasive techniques, identify how adverts target particular audiences and think critically about how media and advertising can influence consumer behaviour.

lessons.title: Diary Writing
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to write effective diary entries before developing their comprehension skills through the wartime diary of a fictional child evacuee during the Second World War.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding the purpose and features of diary writing
✔ Including dates and times in diary entries
✔ Writing consistently in the first person
✔ Using the past tense to recount events
✔ Organising events in chronological order
✔ Selecting important and interesting events to include
✔ Writing from a character's point of view
✔ Expressing personal thoughts, opinions and emotions
✔ Organising diary entries into paragraphs
✔ Writing effective introductions and conclusions
✔ Using an appropriate informal style
✔ Using varied time conjunctions and adverbials
✔ Planning and writing an independent diary entry
✔ Using a checklist to evaluate diary writing
✔ Reading and understanding a wartime diary
✔ Retrieving information from a text
✔ Making inferences about characters' thoughts and feelings
✔ Explaining vocabulary in context
✔ Sequencing events chronologically
✔ Supporting answers with evidence from the text
✔ Comparing how a character's emotions change over time
✔ Explaining an author's choice of diary format
✔ Predicting what might happen next

Students begin by exploring the key conventions of diary writing. They learn that diary entries are personal recounts written from the writer's point of view and usually include a date or time, first-person pronouns, past-tense events and personal thoughts and feelings.

The lesson develops students' understanding of chronological organisation and selecting significant events rather than recording every detail of a day. Students examine how introductions can establish who, what and when, while conclusions can summarise the writer's feelings. They also explore informal language and varied time adverbials such as early this morning, after that and before lunch.

Students then apply these features by planning and writing their own diary entry from the point of view of someone who works with animals. They use a diary-writing checklist to check their use of first person, past tense, chronological order, emotions and time adverbials.

The second part of the lesson develops reading comprehension through The Wartime Diary of Eliza Beale, a fictional child living during the Second World War. Students learn about the uncertainty experienced by evacuated children before reading diary entries describing Eliza and her younger brother George leaving London and travelling to a temporary home.

Through retrieval and inference questions, students investigate Eliza's thoughts, worries and behaviour. They consider why she cannot sleep, why she describes George as lucky, why she hides her name tag and why she gives George her biscuits. Students use evidence from the diary to explain how Eliza responds to being separated from her family.

Students continue by exploring Eliza's arrival at her temporary home, interpreting vocabulary in context, sequencing events and evaluating whether Eliza can be described as brave. They compare her feelings at the beginning and end of the diary, recognising how her uncertainty and fear gradually develop into cautious hope while she remains homesick.

Finally, students consider why the author chose diary entries to tell Eliza's story and predict what she might write next, using evidence from the text to support their ideas.

By the end of the lesson, students will be able to identify and apply the main features of effective diary writing and use retrieval, inference, sequencing, vocabulary and evidence-based reasoning skills to analyse a character's experiences and emotions.
