lessons.title: Persuasive Writing
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how persuasive writing uses carefully chosen language and information to convince a reader to think or act in a particular way.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding the purpose of persuasive writing
✔ Recognising different forms of persuasion, including adverts, speeches and campaigns
✔ Using imperative verbs to tell the reader what to do
✔ Using considered repetition to reinforce important ideas
✔ Using adverbials to engage and influence the reader
✔ Using rhetorical questions effectively
✔ Identifying persuasive techniques in adverts
✔ Analysing persuasive techniques in speeches
✔ Exploring persuasive language in campaigns
✔ Using direct address to speak directly to the reader
✔ Choosing strong and emotive language
✔ Using facts, promises and descriptive language persuasively
✔ Giving clear reasons to support an argument
✔ Writing persuasive letters for different audiences
✔ Creating convincing persuasive adverts
✔ Applying several persuasive techniques within independent writing

Students begin by exploring what persuasion means and considering situations in which they may have tried to convince somebody to agree with them. They learn that effective persuasive writing depends both on the information presented and the language chosen to communicate it.

The lesson introduces four key persuasive techniques: imperative verbs, considered repetition, adverbials and rhetorical questions. Students examine how imperative verbs such as buy and improve give direct instructions, how carefully controlled repetition makes important ideas memorable, how adverbials can strengthen a message and how rhetorical questions engage the reader without requiring an answer.

Students then analyse three different examples of persuasive writing. They investigate an advert and identify rhetorical questions, imperative verbs, repetition and adverbials before examining a persuasive speech in which repetition and powerful language encourage a community to rebuild its home. A campaign speech provides further opportunities to identify repeated promises, positive language, adverbials and direct commands.

The lesson also introduces additional persuasive techniques including direct address, emotive language, facts, promises and carefully chosen descriptive vocabulary. Students consider how these features can work together to make an argument more convincing.

Students then apply their learning through three extended writing activities. In Blast Off, they write a persuasive letter to NASA explaining why they should be allowed to take a phone or tablet on a space mission. In Planet Discovery, they write to their parents to persuade them to allow a journey to a newly discovered planet. In Incredible Inventions, students create an advert designed to persuade customers to buy a futuristic invention.

Throughout these activities, students are encouraged to give clear reasons, consider their audience and deliberately select persuasive techniques rather than simply making unsupported requests.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to recognise and explain a range of persuasive techniques and use imperative verbs, considered repetition, adverbials, rhetorical questions and other persuasive language confidently in their own letters, adverts and arguments.

lessons.title: Descriptive Writing Settings and Atmosphere
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their descriptive writing skills by learning how writers create vivid settings and effective atmospheres. They explore how carefully chosen vocabulary, figurative language and sensory description can help readers visualise a setting and experience its mood.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding setting and atmosphere
✔ Exploring how setting creates mood
✔ Using adjectives and expanded noun phrases
✔ Choosing powerful verbs and adverbs
✔ Using similes and metaphors
✔ Using personification and alliteration
✔ Understanding and applying pathetic fallacy
✔ Describing settings using the five senses
✔ Selecting precise vocabulary to create different atmospheres
✔ Writing and reviewing detailed setting descriptions

Students begin by exploring the difference between setting and atmosphere. They learn that the setting tells the reader where a story takes place, while atmosphere refers to the tone or mood created within that setting.

Students consider how settings in familiar stories can create different feelings, such as excitement, isolation, mystery or danger. They then analyse an atmospheric graveyard extract and identify language that describes the physical setting as well as words and phrases that create an eerie and unsettling mood.

Students will:
✔ Identify details that establish a setting
✔ Recognise vocabulary that creates atmosphere
✔ Analyse adjectives and noun phrases
✔ Identify powerful verb choices
✔ Recognise personification and metaphor
✔ Understand how alliteration can strengthen description
✔ Identify adverbial phrases within descriptive writing

The lesson introduces pathetic fallacy, where weather or nature is used to reflect or reinforce the mood of a scene. Students examine examples such as a moaning wind and consider how natural surroundings can make a setting feel threatening, peaceful, mysterious or tense.

Students then apply these techniques to visual settings. They identify interesting details within images, decide what atmosphere those details could create and write their own setting descriptions using adjectives, noun phrases, powerful verbs, adverbs, similes, metaphors, personification and alliteration. For additional challenge, they incorporate pathetic fallacy.

The lesson also explores how detailed description is more effective than simply stating where a character is. Students compare different descriptions and investigate how precise vocabulary helps readers build a stronger mental picture of a setting.

Students practise describing a range of environments, including an old house, a lagoon, a crowded arena and a setting in space. They consider how individual word choices can make a location appear peaceful, neglected, exciting, threatening or mysterious.

The lesson then focuses on sensory description. Students learn how writers can use sight, sound, smell, touch and feelings to make a setting seem more vivid and immersive.

Students will:
✔ Describe what can be seen within a setting
✔ Include sounds that contribute to the atmosphere
✔ Use smells to make descriptions more immersive
✔ Describe textures and physical sensations
✔ Explain how a setting makes a character feel
✔ Select vocabulary that matches the intended mood

Students apply the five senses to settings including an autumn forest, a beach and a mysterious house. They also explore a vocabulary bank containing precise words for sights, sounds, smells, sensations and emotions.

By the end of the lesson, students will confidently describe settings using powerful and precise vocabulary, use a range of figurative and descriptive techniques, apply the five senses and deliberately create atmosphere for the reader.

lessons.title: Figures of Speech and comprehension
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of figurative language and apply a wide range of reading comprehension skills while exploring the suspense story The Curse of Cogston House.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding figurative language
✔ Identifying similes, metaphors, personification and hyperbole
✔ Explaining the effect of figurative language
✔ Retrieving evidence from a text
✔ Making inferences about characters and settings
✔ Using context to work out unfamiliar vocabulary
✔ Exploring onomatopoeia and rhetorical questions
✔ Identifying grammatical features including adverbs, fronted adverbials and subordinate clauses
✔ Analysing how writers create suspense and atmosphere
✔ Making predictions using evidence from the text
✔ Comparing characters and alternative story endings

Students begin by exploring figurative language and learning that writers often use words in non-literal ways to create stronger images and add emphasis.

They focus on four key figures of speech:
✔ Similes – comparisons using like or as
✔ Metaphors – describing one thing as though it is another
✔ Personification – giving human qualities to non-human things
✔ Hyperbole – deliberate exaggeration for effect

Students practise identifying each technique and explaining how figurative language can make writing more vivid, memorable and expressive.

The lesson then moves into an extended comprehension based on The Curse of Cogston House. Students follow Jack and Luca as they leave the park and investigate a mysterious, abandoned house surrounded by rumours and strange stories.

Students will:
✔ Infer personality traits from characters' actions and dialogue
✔ Support answers with evidence from the text
✔ Compare the contrasting personalities of Jack and Luca
✔ Form impressions of Cogston House from descriptive details
✔ Interpret expressions and phrases using context
✔ Identify figurative language within a narrative
✔ Explain how vocabulary contributes to atmosphere

Students encounter ambitious vocabulary including undeterred, decrepit, solemnly, traipsed and trepidation and use contextual clues to work out meanings.

The story introduces the mystery of Alice and Eliza, two girls who previously explored Cogston House. Students examine how descriptions, repeated clock sounds and unusual details gradually build tension and reveal the house's sinister history.

Students explore a range of writing and structural techniques, including:
✔ Similes and metaphors
✔ Personification
✔ Onomatopoeia
✔ Short sentences for dramatic effect
✔ Repetition
✔ Ellipsis
✔ Rhetorical questions
✔ Sentence spacing and paragraph breaks
✔ Physical descriptions of fear
✔ Delayed revelation to build suspense

Students analyse how repeated sounds such as tick and tick tock slow the pace, create rhythm and increase tension. They also investigate clues surrounding the repeated time of ten thirty one and connect events from Jack's story with what is happening to Luca in the present.

The lesson requires students to make increasingly sophisticated inferences and predictions. They explain how characters are feeling, identify evidence of fear, interpret mysterious clues and predict what may happen based on events that have already occurred.

Students also examine grammatical features within the story, including fronted adverbials, subordinate clauses and adverbs, and consider how these contribute to meaning and atmosphere.

Towards the end of the lesson, students compare Jack and Luca's reactions to danger and investigate the escalating suspense as the boys discover a row of grandfather clocks inside Cogston House.

The story then offers two possible endings: Out to Safety and Under the Curse. Students explore both outcomes, make inferences about the mysterious figure in the house, compare the effectiveness of the endings and explain which version they prefer.

By the end of the lesson, students will confidently identify and explain a range of figures of speech, retrieve and infer information from an extended narrative, use contextual clues to understand vocabulary, analyse suspense techniques and support their comprehension responses with evidence from the text.

lessons.description:

They explore how reports present factual information clearly and how different sections can be organised under suitable subheadings without needing to follow a chronological order. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding the purpose of non-chronological reports
✔ Planning a report before writing
✔ Choosing an appropriate title
✔ Organising information into clear sections
✔ Using subheadings effectively
✔ Selecting key facts for each section
✔ Using technical vocabulary
✔ Creating and using Spidergrams
✔ Writing in the present tense
✔ Reviewing and editing report writing

Students begin by learning that a non-chronological report presents information about a topic without needing to follow a particular time order. Instead, information is grouped into different subject areas, with each section focusing on a different aspect of the topic.

The lesson then introduces a five-step planning process. Students first choose a title and place the main topic at the centre of their plan. They then organise the information into different sections and create suitable subheadings.

Students will:
✔ Identify useful subject areas for a report
✔ Include an introduction
✔ Group related information together
✔ Add key facts beneath each subheading
✔ Plan using notes rather than full sentences
✔ Add useful technical and descriptive vocabulary

Students are introduced to a Spidergram as an effective way of organising ideas before writing. A model report about guinea pigs demonstrates how information can be divided into sections such as appearance, diet, habitat and interesting facts. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

The lesson also focuses on the features students should check when writing a finished report. These include using an appropriate title, clear subheadings, relevant information, technical vocabulary, present tense, capital letters and full stops. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}

Students then explore another Spidergram based on sports and see how a broad topic can be divided into smaller categories such as individual sports, water sports, contact sports and team sports.

They next practise converting information from a report about the Pyramids of Ancient Egypt into a Spidergram. Possible sections include tombs, the Sphinx, the Pyramid of Djoser, the Pyramids of Giza and hieroglyphics.

Finally, students create their own Spidergram about India. lessons.title: Punctuation Quiz, Verbal Reasoning and Comprehension
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their punctuation accuracy, verbal reasoning skills and reading comprehension through a varied set of activities.

This lesson includes:
✔ Using commas after opening phrases and in lists
✔ Using commas, brackets and dashes for parenthesis
✔ Using apostrophes for plural possession
✔ Punctuating direct speech accurately
✔ Solving Moving Letters verbal reasoning questions
✔ Retrieving information from a non-fiction text
✔ Explaining vocabulary choices using context
✔ Making inferences and giving evidence-based answers

Students begin with a punctuation quiz covering commas, brackets, dashes, apostrophes and direct speech. They identify correctly punctuated sentences and explain how punctuation is used to separate opening phrases, list items and additional information. They also practise placing apostrophes correctly for plural possession and using inverted commas, commas, full stops and question marks accurately within direct speech.

The verbal reasoning section introduces Moving Letters. Students move one letter from a five-letter word to a three-letter word to create two new four-letter words while keeping the remaining letters in their original order. This develops vocabulary, spelling, letter manipulation and systematic reasoning skills.

The lesson then moves to reading comprehension using an informative passage about the Sun. Students retrieve facts about the Sun's composition, energy, layers and gravity, while also tackling vocabulary, explanation and inference questions.

Students explore scientific information including hydrogen and helium, the Sun's layers, solar terminology, the role of gravity in the Solar System and what may eventually happen to the Sun. They also answer open-ended questions requiring them to use information from the text alongside sensible reasoning.

By the end of the lesson, students will have strengthened their punctuation knowledge, developed verbal reasoning strategies and practised retrieving, interpreting and explaining information from a non-fiction text.

lessons.title: Instructional reports
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to write clear and effective instruction texts. They explore the purpose, organisation and language features of instructions before applying their learning to a creative magical plant activity.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding the purpose of instruction texts
✔ Identifying where instructions are used in everyday life
✔ Using clear titles and subheadings
✔ Listing materials, ingredients or equipment
✔ Organising steps in chronological order
✔ Using numbers and bullet points
✔ Using time conjunctions to sequence instructions
✔ Using imperative verbs and adverbs
✔ Writing short, clear sentences
✔ Using diagrams and labelled illustrations
✔ Including warnings, tips and additional advice
✔ Planning instructions for a magical greenhouse plant

Students begin by exploring different situations where instructions are needed, including recipes, games, craft activities and safety procedures. They consider why instructions need to be clear, organised and presented in a logical sequence.

Students examine examples including How to Plant a Sunflower Seed and How to Make Fruit Pizzas. They identify important organisational features such as a clear title, a list of things needed and individual steps arranged in the correct order.

The lesson focuses on time conjunctions including first, next, then, now, after that and finally. Students also explore imperative or command verbs such as mix, stir, place, add, pour, cut and cover, and learn how adverbs can provide additional detail about how an action should be completed.

Students then apply their learning through a creative task based around magical greenhouse plants. They invent their own magical plant, considering its appearance, magical properties and any unusual care or growing requirements it might have.

Using Mandrakes as a model, students analyse a detailed instruction text and identify titles, subheadings, introductions, equipment lists, chronological steps, labelled illustrations, imperative verbs, time conjunctions, adverbs, warnings, top tips and conclusions.

By the end of the lesson, students will understand how effective instruction texts are structured and will be able to use organisational and language features to plan and write clear, engaging instructions of their own.

lessons.title: Verbal Reasoning
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop a broad range of verbal reasoning skills by working systematically with words, letters, vocabulary, patterns and codes.

This lesson includes:
✔ Creating compound words from pairs of smaller words
✔ Inserting missing letters to complete two words simultaneously
✔ Finding smaller words hidden within larger words
✔ Inserting three-letter words to complete longer words in sentences
✔ Moving letters between words to create two new words
✔ Identifying words with opposite meanings
✔ Solving alphabet-based word codes
✔ Recognising changing and alternating letter patterns
✔ Encoding and decoding words using systematic rules
✔ Identifying two odd words out from groups of five
✔ Recognising relationships between words
✔ Developing vocabulary, spelling and logical reasoning skills

Students begin by creating compound words from two groups of words. They combine pairs to form correctly spelt words such as blackberry, pumpkin, firework, chestnut, evergreen, haystack, hedgehog, raindrop, cobweb and firecracker.

The lesson then develops letter manipulation skills. Students identify a single letter that can simultaneously complete one word and begin another, before finding smaller words that can be constructed using only the letters available within a larger word.

Students next tackle missing-word problems in which a three-letter word must be inserted into an incomplete word to create a longer word that correctly completes a sentence. Examples develop careful attention to spelling, vocabulary and context.

The Moving Letters section requires students to transfer one letter from the first word to the second while preserving the order of all remaining letters. Both resulting letter sequences must form valid new words. Students work through examples such as acorn and red becoming corn and read, chill and old becoming hill and cold, and brisk and right becoming risk and bright.

Students then strengthen their vocabulary by identifying pairs of words with opposite meanings, including new and old, awake and asleep, near and far, combine and separate, create and destroy, dangerous and safe, enter and exit, and come and go.

The lesson progresses to increasingly challenging word-code problems. Students analyse how letters have moved through the alphabet, identify the underlying rule and apply or reverse that rule to encode and decode new words. Patterns include alternating movements, increasing shifts, decreasing shifts and repeated sequences.

Finally, students solve odd-one-out questions. For each group of five words, they identify the three words that share a meaningful relationship and select the remaining two as the odd ones out. These activities require careful consideration of categories, meanings and associations rather than simply recognising superficial similarities.

By the end of the lesson, students will have strengthened their verbal reasoning through compound words, letter manipulation, vocabulary relationships, word construction, alphabet codes and classification problems, while developing systematic strategies for tackling unfamiliar reasoning questions.

lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to read, write, and represent numbers up to one million.
They use place value grids, counters, and models to understand how digit positions affect value.

This lesson includes:
✔ Representing numbers in different ways
✔ Standard and non-standard partitioning
✔ Reading and writing large numbers
✔ Finding the value of digits
✔ Comparing place values

lessons.title: Fractions 2
lessons.description:

They use equivalent fractions and visual models to order fractions accurately.

This lesson includes:
✔ Fraction number sequences
✔ Converting mixed and improper fractions
✔ Comparing fractions using models
✔ Finding common denominators
✔ Simplifying fractions

lessons.title: Fractions 3
lessons.description:

✔ Using common denominators and numerators

lessons.title: Fractions 4
lessons.description:
In this 11+ lesson, students order fractions greater than one and compare improper fractions and mixed numbers.

✔ Fraction counting sticks for fluency
✔ Adding and subtracting fractions with the same denominator
✔ Converting improper answers into mixed numbers
✔ Missing number and reasoning problems

✔ Adding fractions with denominator multiples using equivalent fractions
✔ Adding three fractions efficiently

✔ True or false and error spotting tasks
✔ Fraction word problems
✔ Adding fractions that cross one whole

lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to describe position using coordinates and explore lines of symmetry in shapes. They practise reading coordinates correctly by moving across the x-axis first and then up the y-axis, solving missing coordinate problems, and identifying symmetrical shapes.

✔ Understanding the x-axis (across) and y-axis (up)
✔ Solving missing coordinate problems on a grid
✔ Using coordinates to locate objects on a map
✔ Understanding regular and irregular shapes
✔ Identifying vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines of symmetry
✔ Counting lines of symmetry in regular polygons
✔ Reasoning about symmetry using folding and mirror tests

lessons.title: Reflection
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how to draw and identify reflected shapes using mirror lines and coordinates.

✔ Checking whether a reflection is correct
✔ Drawing reflected shapes accurately
✔ Keeping equal distance from the mirror line
✔ Identifying missing coordinates after reflection
✔ Solving reflection reasoning problems

lessons.title: Properties of Shapes 1
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of angles, turns and angle measurement in degrees. They learn how to classify, measure and interpret angles using protractors, compass directions and real-life contexts.

Students begin by revising acute, right and obtuse angles.
They learn how to identify and classify angles according to their size.

Students will:
✔ Recognise acute, right and obtuse angles
✔ Explain why angles belong to each category
✔ Compare different angle sizes
✔ Draw examples of different angle types

The lesson then explores clockwise and anticlockwise turns.
Students learn how turns relate to the movement of clock hands.

Students will also:
✔ Identify clockwise and anticlockwise rotations
✔ Describe turns using mathematical vocabulary
✔ Compare different directions of rotation
✔ Apply turning language in practical situations

Next, students learn how turns are measured in degrees.
They investigate quarter turns, half turns, three-quarter turns and full turns.

Students will:
✔ Understand that a quarter turn is 90°
✔ Understand that a half turn is 180°
✔ Understand that a three-quarter turn is 270°
✔ Understand that a full turn is 360°
✔ Link turns to angle types

The lesson then introduces angle classification using degree measures.
Students learn that:
✔ Acute angles are less than 90°
✔ Right angles measure exactly 90°
✔ Obtuse angles are greater than 90° and less than 180°
✔ Straight line angles measure 180°
✔ Reflex angles are greater than 180° and less than 360°
✔ Full angles measure 360°

Students also explore compass directions and bearings.
They use compass points to calculate turns and identify angle sizes.

Students will:
✔ Measure angles between compass points
✔ Use 45° intervals between neighbouring compass directions
✔ Calculate clockwise and anticlockwise turns
✔ Classify compass angles as acute, obtuse or reflex
✔ Solve direction and movement problems

Next, students investigate real-life turning scenarios.
They use maps, landmarks and compass directions to work out where someone will be facing after a turn.

Students will also:
✔ Calculate turning angles accurately
✔ Follow directional instructions
✔ Predict final positions after rotations
✔ Apply angle reasoning in context

The lesson then introduces measuring acute angles using a protractor.
Students learn how to position a protractor correctly and read the appropriate scale.

Students will:
✔ Identify the vertex of an angle
✔ Align the protractor accurately
✔ Read angles from inside and outside scales
✔ Measure acute angles to the nearest degree
✔ Estimate angles before measuring

Students then learn how to measure obtuse angles.

They will:
✔ Use a protractor to measure obtuse angles
✔ Choose the correct scale on the protractor
✔ Measure angles accurately between labelled intervals
✔ Read precise angle measurements using degree increments
✔ Check whether answers are reasonable

The lesson also develops estimation and reasoning skills.
Students learn how estimating first helps identify mistakes when reading a protractor.

Students will:
✔ Estimate angle sizes before measuring
✔ Spot incorrect measurements
✔ Explain common protractor errors
✔ Use angle knowledge to justify answers
✔ Compare reasonable and unreasonable measurements

Finally, students solve reasoning problems involving angle measurement.
They identify mistakes, explain misconceptions and apply their understanding of angle types and degree measures.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently classify angles, measure acute and obtuse angles using a protractor, calculate turns in degrees, and apply angle knowledge to solve a wide range of reasoning and direction problems.
lessons.subject: maths

lessons.title: Properties of Shapes 2
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students deepen their understanding of angle relationships by exploring angles on a straight line and angles around a point. They learn how to use known angle facts to calculate missing angles and solve reasoning problems.

Students begin by revising key angle facts.
They learn that a straight angle measures 180° and is equivalent to a half turn.

Students will:
✔ Recognise that a straight line angle measures 180°
✔ Link straight angles to half turns
✔ Understand that two right angles make 180°
✔ Use angle facts to support calculations
✔ Compare different angle sizes

The lesson then focuses on angles on a straight line.
Students learn that all angles on a straight line add up to 180°.

Students will:
✔ Calculate missing angles on a straight line
✔ Use subtraction to find unknown angles
✔ Solve problems with two and three adjacent angles
✔ Identify acute, right and obtuse missing angles
✔ Check answers using inverse operations

Students also use bar models and number lines to visualise angle calculations.

They will:
✔ Represent angle totals using bar models
✔ Use known and unknown parts of a whole
✔ Apply addition and subtraction strategies
✔ Explain their reasoning clearly
✔ Verify solutions efficiently

Next, students revisit angle types.
They classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight line and reflex angles.

Students will:
✔ Identify different types of angles
✔ Compare angle sizes accurately
✔ Use degree measurements to justify classifications
✔ Recall key angle definitions
✔ Apply angle vocabulary confidently

The lesson then introduces angles around a point.
Students learn that angles around a point always total 360°.

Students will:
✔ Understand that angles around a point equal a full turn
✔ Link 360° to four right angles
✔ Recognise full-turn angle relationships
✔ Use angle facts to solve problems
✔ Interpret diagrams involving complete rotations

Students then calculate missing angles around a point.
They use known angle values to determine unknown angles.

Students will:
✔ Calculate missing angles using subtraction
✔ Solve problems involving three or more angles
✔ Work with acute, obtuse and reflex missing angles
✔ Use inverse operations to check answers
✔ Explain how they found solutions

The lesson also develops reasoning and problem-solving skills.
Students compare questions, identify similarities and differences, and decide which angle facts apply.

Students will:
✔ Spot patterns in angle problems
✔ Select appropriate solving strategies
✔ Justify calculations mathematically
✔ Explain mistakes and misconceptions
✔ Solve increasingly complex angle challenges

Finally, students apply their understanding to mixed missing-angle problems involving straight lines and points.
They combine angle facts, arithmetic and logical reasoning to find unknown values.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently calculate missing angles on straight lines and around points, apply key angle facts, and solve a wide range of angle reasoning problems.

lessons.title: Properties of Shapes 3
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students apply their knowledge of shape properties to calculate missing lengths, find unknown angles, classify polygons, and investigate three-dimensional shapes and shape nets.

Students begin by solving perimeter problems involving regular and compound shapes.
They use known side lengths and shape properties to calculate missing measurements.

This lesson includes:
✔ Calculating the perimeter of regular and irregular shapes
✔ Finding missing side lengths using known measurements
✔ Using properties of rectangles and squares
✔ Solving perimeter problems involving compound shapes
✔ Applying logical reasoning to real-life contexts

The lesson then develops angle reasoning within shapes.
Students use angle facts to calculate unknown angles in squares, triangles, and composite figures.

Students will:
✔ Calculate missing angles in shapes
✔ Use the fact that angles on a straight line total 180°
✔ Use the fact that angles in a triangle total 180°
✔ Apply properties of isosceles triangles
✔ Use right-angle facts to solve problems efficiently

Students also learn how complex shapes can be broken into simpler shapes to support problem-solving.

They will:
✔ Split compound shapes into rectangles and triangles
✔ Find missing angles using known angle facts
✔ Combine angle calculations from different parts of a shape
✔ Explain their mathematical reasoning
✔ Solve multi-step geometry problems

Next, students explore polygons.
They learn what makes a shape a polygon and how polygons can be classified.

Students will:
✔ Identify polygons and non-polygons
✔ Recognise that polygons must be closed shapes
✔ Understand that polygons must have straight sides
✔ Classify shapes using geometric properties
✔ Justify why shapes belong in particular groups

The lesson then introduces regular and irregular polygons.
Students investigate the properties that make a polygon regular.

Students will:
✔ Understand that regular polygons have equal sides and equal angles
✔ Compare regular and irregular polygons
✔ Identify common regular polygons
✔ Investigate properties of different triangles
✔ Recognise that only equilateral triangles are regular polygons

Students then move on to three-dimensional shapes.
They identify and classify a range of common solids.

Students will:
✔ Recognise cubes, cuboids, prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones and spheres
✔ Identify octahedrons and triangular prisms
✔ Compare different three-dimensional shapes
✔ Describe geometric properties accurately
✔ Use correct mathematical vocabulary

The lesson also introduces polyhedrons.
Students learn how to distinguish polyhedrons from shapes with curved surfaces.

Students will:
✔ Understand that polyhedrons have flat faces, straight edges and vertices
✔ Classify three-dimensional shapes as polyhedrons or non-polyhedrons
✔ Identify faces, edges and vertices
✔ Explain why cylinders, cones and spheres are not polyhedrons
✔ Apply geometric reasoning to classification tasks

Finally, students explore shape nets.
They learn how two-dimensional nets fold into three-dimensional shapes.

Students will:
✔ Identify valid and invalid shape nets
✔ Recognise nets of cubes, cuboids, prisms and octahedrons
✔ Count faces in three-dimensional shapes
✔ Match two-dimensional faces to three-dimensional solids
✔ Visualise how shapes fold together

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently calculate lengths and angles in shapes, classify regular and irregular polygons, identify three-dimensional shapes and polyhedrons, and interpret and construct shape nets.

lessons.title: Measurement 1
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of perimeter by measuring accurately, converting between units of length, and solving increasingly complex perimeter problems involving rectangles, rectilinear shapes, polygons, and composite figures.

Students begin by exploring equivalent measurements and using rulers correctly.
They learn how centimetres, millimetres, and decimal measurements are connected.

This lesson includes:
✔ Converting between centimetres and millimetres
✔ Reading measurements accurately from a ruler
✔ Identifying common measuring mistakes
✔ Writing equivalent measurements in different forms
✔ Using decimal notation for lengths

The lesson then introduces the perimeter of rectangles.
Students learn multiple methods for calculating perimeter and compare the efficiency of different approaches.

Students will:
✔ Understand perimeter as the distance around a shape
✔ Calculate the perimeter of rectangles
✔ Use addition and multiplication methods
✔ Compare different calculation strategies
✔ Solve perimeter problems involving decimal lengths

Students also investigate missing side lengths in rectangles.
They use perimeter information to calculate unknown dimensions.

Students will:
✔ Find missing lengths using known perimeters
✔ Apply inverse operations
✔ Solve reasoning problems involving rectangles
✔ Explore multiple rectangles with the same perimeter
✔ Recognise patterns between perimeter, length, and width

The lesson then extends to rectilinear shapes.
Students learn how to calculate perimeters when shapes contain many sides and missing measurements.

Students will:
✔ Calculate the perimeter of rectilinear shapes
✔ Identify and calculate missing side lengths
✔ Use addition and subtraction to determine unknown measurements
✔ Apply perimeter reasoning to compound shapes
✔ Develop efficient calculation strategies

Students explore reasoning and problem-solving questions involving perimeter.
They learn that some shapes can be solved even when individual measurements are not known.

Students will:
✔ Use total horizontal and vertical lengths to find perimeter
✔ Determine when enough information is available
✔ Justify mathematical conclusions
✔ Solve multi-step perimeter problems
✔ Apply logical geometric reasoning

The lesson also investigates shapes made from identical squares.
Students examine how arrangement affects perimeter.

Students will:
✔ Calculate the perimeter of composite shapes made from squares
✔ Determine square dimensions from a known perimeter
✔ Count perimeter edges efficiently
✔ Compare different arrangements of identical shapes
✔ Understand how shape structure affects perimeter

Next, students explore the perimeter of polygons.
They learn how regular polygons can be calculated efficiently using multiplication.

Students will:
✔ Identify polygons and regular polygons
✔ Calculate the perimeter of regular polygons
✔ Use the number of sides and side length to find perimeter
✔ Find missing side lengths from a known perimeter
✔ Solve reasoning problems involving regular shapes

The lesson then develops perimeter reasoning using compound polygon arrangements.
Students investigate how joining shapes changes the perimeter.

Students will:
✔ Calculate the perimeter of combined shapes
✔ Recognise that shared edges are internal and not part of the perimeter
✔ Compare different solution methods
✔ Use subtraction to account for shared boundaries
✔ Solve real-life perimeter problems involving joined shapes

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently measure lengths, convert between centimetres and millimetres, calculate the perimeter of rectangles, rectilinear shapes and polygons, find missing side lengths, and solve complex perimeter reasoning problems.

lessons.title: Measurement 2
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of area by calculating, comparing, estimating, and solving problems involving rectangles, compound shapes, and irregular shapes.

Students begin by exploring what area represents and why it is useful in everyday life.
They learn that area measures the amount of space inside a two-dimensional shape and is measured using square units.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding area as the space inside a shape
✔ Recognising real-life uses of area
✔ Understanding square centimetres and square metres
✔ Linking arrays to area calculations
✔ Comparing different arrangements with the same area

Students first calculate area by counting squares.
They learn how square units measure surface area and how counting can be used to find the area of simple shapes.

Students will:
✔ Count square units accurately
✔ Calculate area using square centimetres
✔ Recognise area as a measure of surface coverage
✔ Compare areas of different shapes
✔ Record answers using correct units

The lesson then introduces the area formula for rectangles.
Students learn how multiplication can be used to calculate area efficiently.

Students will:
✔ Use the formula area = length × width
✔ Calculate areas of rectangles
✔ Work with measurements in centimetres and metres
✔ Choose appropriate square units
✔ Solve practical area problems

Students explore reasoning and error-spotting activities.
They learn to identify common mistakes involving area calculations and units.

Students will:
✔ Check calculations for accuracy
✔ Identify incorrect methods
✔ Distinguish between perimeter and area
✔ Use correct units of measurement
✔ Justify mathematical reasoning

The lesson also develops understanding of factors and area relationships.
Students investigate how different rectangles can have the same area.

Students will:
✔ Find factor pairs of a number
✔ Create rectangles with a given area
✔ Explore links between multiplication and area
✔ Compare different rectangle dimensions
✔ Apply reasoning to area investigations

Students are then introduced to compound shapes.
They learn how complex shapes can be divided into simpler rectangles.

Students will:
✔ Understand what compound and composite shapes are
✔ Split compound shapes into rectangles
✔ Calculate the area of each section
✔ Add areas together to find totals
✔ Solve multi-step area problems

The lesson also introduces the subtraction method for compound shapes.
Students learn how to calculate a larger rectangle and remove missing sections.

Students will:
✔ Calculate the area of larger enclosing rectangles
✔ Find areas of missing sections
✔ Use subtraction to determine compound shape areas
✔ Compare different solution methods
✔ Solve real-life area problems involving gardens, ponds, and layouts

Students explore more advanced area reasoning.
They calculate fractional areas and solve problems involving overlapping calculations.

Students will:
✔ Use fractions of known areas
✔ Apply area calculations to real-world scenarios
✔ Interpret diagrams efficiently
✔ Solve multi-step reasoning problems
✔ Justify mathematical conclusions

The lesson then introduces estimating area.
Students learn how to estimate the area of irregular shapes using square grids.

Students will:
✔ Estimate areas using whole squares
✔ Combine partial squares to create whole squares
✔ Understand acceptable ranges for estimates
✔ Compare different estimation methods
✔ Develop efficient counting strategies

Students also distinguish between exact and estimated area.
They learn when exact answers are possible and when estimation is more appropriate.

Students will:
✔ Identify exact areas using whole and half squares
✔ Estimate areas of irregular shapes
✔ Recognise when estimation is required
✔ Evaluate the accuracy of estimates
✔ Explain reasoning using mathematical language

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently calculate the area of rectangles and compound shapes, solve real-life area problems, understand square units, estimate the area of irregular shapes, and apply area reasoning in a variety of mathematical contexts.

lessons.title: Counting in Powers of Ten
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students explore powers of ten and how numbers change when multiplied or divided by ten, one hundred, and one thousand.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding powers of ten
✔ Counting forwards and backwards in steps
✔ Using place value grids
✔ Solving number sequences
✔ Reasoning with patterns

lessons.title: Measurement 3
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop fluency with metric and imperial measurement conversions, learning how prefixes help us understand relationships between units and how conversion skills can be applied to solve real-life problems.

Students begin by exploring the meaning of the metric prefixes kilo and milli.
They learn how these prefixes help us understand the size relationships between different units of measurement.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding the meaning of kilo and milli
✔ Exploring relationships between metric units
✔ Using place value when converting measurements
✔ Reading and interpreting number lines
✔ Applying conversion rules in practical contexts

Students first learn about kilograms and grams.
They investigate how mass can be converted between larger and smaller metric units.

Students will:
✔ Convert kilograms to grams
✔ Convert grams to kilograms
✔ Use multiplication and division by one thousand
✔ Interpret number lines involving mass
✔ Solve practical mass problems

The lesson then develops understanding of decimal conversions.
Students learn how decimal values relate to metric measurements.

Students will:
✔ Convert decimal kilograms into grams
✔ Interpret values between whole numbers
✔ Use tenths and halves on number lines
✔ Compare equivalent measurements
✔ Recognise patterns in metric conversions

Students then apply the same principles to kilometres and metres.
They learn how distance measurements follow identical conversion rules.

Students will:
✔ Convert kilometres to metres
✔ Convert metres to kilometres
✔ Use multiplication and division by one thousand
✔ Read distance scales and number lines
✔ Solve distance conversion problems

The lesson introduces millimetres and metres.
Students investigate how smaller units relate to larger metric units.

Students will:
✔ Convert metres into millimetres
✔ Convert millimetres into metres
✔ Work with decimal values and fractions
✔ Use place value knowledge when converting
✔ Solve practical measurement questions

Students then learn about litres and millilitres.
They explore capacity conversions using both whole numbers and decimals.

Students will:
✔ Convert litres into millilitres
✔ Convert millilitres into litres
✔ Interpret decimal capacities
✔ Use number lines to represent capacity
✔ Solve real-life capacity problems

The lesson develops understanding of equivalent measurements involving fractions and decimals.
Students use reasoning to connect metric units.

Students will:
✔ Convert fractional metres into millimetres
✔ Convert decimal litres into millilitres
✔ Compare equivalent measurements
✔ Apply proportional reasoning
✔ Interpret measurement scales accurately

Students then compare different metric units.
They learn to convert measurements into a common unit before comparing values.

Students will:
✔ Compare measurements given in different units
✔ Identify and correct conversion errors
✔ Convert between millimetres, centimetres and metres
✔ Explain mathematical reasoning
✔ Spot common misconceptions

The lesson also introduces imperial units.
Students learn commonly used approximate conversions between metric and imperial systems.

Students will:
✔ Convert inches and centimetres approximately
✔ Convert kilograms and pounds approximately
✔ Convert pints and millilitres approximately
✔ Understand the meaning of approximate equivalence
✔ Use practical conversion facts efficiently

Students explore scaling strategies and proportional reasoning.
They use doubling, halving and known facts to estimate equivalent values.

Students will:
✔ Apply multiplicative reasoning
✔ Use known benchmark conversions
✔ Estimate measurements efficiently
✔ Compare metric and imperial quantities
✔ Justify answers using conversion facts

The lesson concludes with multi-step reasoning problems involving mixed units.
Students solve practical scenarios by converting measurements into common units before comparing them.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently convert between kilograms and grams, kilometres and metres, millimetres and metres, litres and millilitres, compare metric measurements, use approximate imperial conversions, and solve real-life measurement problems involving a range of units.

lessons.title: Measurement 4
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of time, timetables, capacity and volume. They learn how to convert between units of time, interpret timetables, estimate capacities, and calculate the volume of cubes and cuboids.

Students begin by exploring relationships between units of time.
They learn how multiplication and division can be used to convert between different time units.

This lesson includes:
✔ Converting between seconds, minutes and hours
✔ Converting between days, weeks, months and years
✔ Solving time conversion problems
✔ Interpreting timetables
✔ Estimating capacity and volume

Students first investigate seconds and minutes.
They learn how to convert between these units using multiplication and division.

Students will:
✔ Convert minutes into seconds
✔ Convert seconds into minutes
✔ Use multiplication and division by sixty
✔ Apply known multiplication facts
✔ Solve real-life time problems

The lesson then develops understanding of hours and minutes.
Students learn how larger units of time relate to smaller units.

Students will:
✔ Convert hours into minutes
✔ Convert minutes into hours
✔ Use multiplication and division by sixty
✔ Compare durations accurately
✔ Solve multi-step time calculations

Students explore practical time problems involving durations.
They learn how to compare times expressed in different formats.

Students will:
✔ Convert mixed units of time
✔ Compare race times and event durations
✔ Calculate differences between times
✔ Use reasoning to justify answers
✔ Apply inverse operations when converting

The lesson introduces days, weeks, months and years.
Students use multiplication and division facts to convert between longer periods of time.

Students will:
✔ Convert weeks into days
✔ Convert days into weeks
✔ Convert years into months
✔ Convert months into years
✔ Compare ages using equivalent units

Students then develop their timetable skills.
They learn how to read, interpret and use timetable information.

Students will:
✔ Read bus and train timetables
✔ Identify departure and arrival times
✔ Determine earliest and latest journeys
✔ Interpret timetable symbols and conventions
✔ Extract relevant information efficiently

The lesson develops duration calculations using timetables.
Students learn how to calculate journey times accurately.

Students will:
✔ Calculate durations between times

They learn how to combine timetable information with time conversions.

Students will:
✔ Solve multi-step timetable problems

✔ Determine suitable travel options
✔ Explain mathematical reasoning
✔ Avoid common errors when working with time

The lesson then introduces estimating capacity.
Students learn the difference between capacity and volume and how to estimate sensible capacities for everyday objects.

Students will:
✔ Understand the meaning of capacity
✔ Estimate realistic capacities
✔ Select appropriate units of measure
✔ Compare container sizes
✔ Apply measurement knowledge to everyday contexts

Students next explore volume.
They learn that volume measures the amount of space occupied by a three-dimensional object.

✔ Compare volumes of different shapes
✔ Recognise hidden cubes in structures

They explore the relationship between scaling dimensions and resulting volumes.

Students will:
✔ Predict changes in volume
✔ Calculate volumes after scaling dimensions
✔ Compare original and enlarged shapes
✔ Use multiplicative reasoning
✔ Explain patterns in volume calculations

The lesson concludes with reasoning and problem-solving involving cuboids.
Students investigate missing cubes, complete cuboids, and explore different dimension combinations that produce the same volume.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently convert between units of time, interpret and use timetables, estimate capacities, distinguish between capacity and volume, calculate volumes of cubes and cuboids, and solve a wide range of practical measurement problems.

lessons.description:
In this lesson, students learn how hyphens are used to join words or parts of words and make writing clearer by avoiding confusion.

This lesson includes:
✔ Recognising hyphens in words and phrases
✔ Using hyphens in compound adjectives such as hot-pink and bear-like
✔ Joining nouns to form compound nouns or adjectives
✔ Using hyphens with prefixes to avoid awkward vowel combinations, such as co-operate and de-escalate

Students begin by learning what a hyphen is and how this small punctuation mark can change meaning. They identify hyphens in context and explain why each one has been used, then explore compound adjectives, compound nouns, prefixes, written numbers, line breaks and informal expressions.

By the end of the lesson, learners will understand the main purposes of hyphens and be able to use them more accurately to make their writing clearer.

lessons.title: Transformations 2
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop advanced transformation skills by translating and reflecting shapes on four-quadrant coordinate grids. They learn to describe translations using coordinate notation, identify reflections across the x-axis and y-axis, determine missing coordinates through logical reasoning, and solve challenging multi-step transformation problems.

This lesson includes:
✔ Translating shapes in all four quadrants
✔ Writing translations using coordinate notation
✔ Reflecting shapes in the x-axis and y-axis
✔ Finding missing coordinates after transformations
✔ Solving multi-step transformation reasoning problems

Students begin by translating shapes on four-quadrant coordinate grids.

Students will:
✔ Translate shapes left, right, up and down
✔ Move every vertex by the same amount
✔ Understand that translations preserve size and orientation
✔ Label successive transformations using prime notation
✔ Describe translations accurately

The lesson then introduces translation vectors using coordinate notation.

Students will:
✔ Write translations using ordered pairs
✔ Understand positive and negative movement along each axis
✔ Link horizontal movement to the x-axis
✔ Link vertical movement to the y-axis
✔ Apply translation coordinates to every vertex

Students then apply translation reasoning to coordinate geometry.

Students will:
✔ Identify missing coordinates after translations
✔ Determine translation vectors from known points
✔ Solve coordinate reasoning questions
✔ Use algebraic reasoning to calculate unknown vertices
✔ Check answers logically

The lesson then explores reflections on coordinate grids.

Students will:
✔ Identify correct and incorrect reflections
✔ Recognise mirror images
✔ Reflect shapes across horizontal, vertical and diagonal mirror lines
✔ Understand congruency after reflection
✔ Explain why reflected shapes remain the same size and shape

Students extend their understanding by reflecting shapes across the x-axis and y-axis.

Students will:
✔ Reflect coordinates across the x-axis
✔ Reflect coordinates across the y-axis
✔ Identify which coordinate changes sign
✔ Find missing reflected vertices
✔ Solve reflection reasoning problems

The lesson concludes with advanced reasoning questions that combine translation, reflection and coordinate geometry. Students solve missing-coordinate problems, complete transformed shapes, describe transformation rules, and justify each stage of their reasoning using mathematical vocabulary.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently translate and reflect shapes on four-quadrant coordinate grids, describe transformations using coordinate notation, determine missing coordinates through logical reasoning, and solve complex transformation problems involving multiple steps.

lessons.title: Properties of Shapes 1
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of the properties of two-dimensional shapes, accurate geometrical drawing, angle measurement, and angle reasoning. They learn how to use mathematical equipment correctly, calculate interior angles of polygons, and solve problems involving angles around a point.

This lesson includes:
✔ Drawing and measuring two-dimensional shapes accurately
✔ Using rulers and protractors correctly
✔ Calculating interior angles of polygons
✔ Identifying and classifying different types of angles
✔ Solving problems involving angles at a point

Students begin by revisiting the area of rectangles and squares before developing accurate drawing skills.

Students will:
✔ Calculate the area of rectangles and squares
✔ Measure lengths accurately using rulers
✔ Draw straight lines to precise measurements
✔ Understand centimetres and millimetres
✔ Develop accurate geometrical drawing skills

The lesson then focuses on using a protractor.
Students learn how to measure and draw angles precisely.

Students will:
✔ Identify the vertex of an angle
✔ Position a protractor correctly
✔ Read the correct scale
✔ Measure angles in degrees
✔ Draw given angles accurately

Students explore the interior angles of polygons.
They discover how polygons can be divided into triangles and use this pattern to calculate angle sums.

Students will:
✔ Divide polygons into triangles
✔ Find the interior angle sum of quadrilaterals
✔ Calculate interior angle sums of pentagons and hexagons
✔ Recognise patterns between number of sides and angle sums
✔ Use the formula (n − 2) × 180° to calculate interior angles of polygons

The lesson develops students' understanding of angle types.
Students identify angles using both their appearance and their measurements.

Students will:
✔ Identify acute angles
✔ Identify obtuse angles
✔ Identify reflex angles
✔ Recognise right angles
✔ Recognise straight angles

Students then investigate angle facts.
They learn how rotations affect angles and apply known angle relationships.

Students will:
✔ Understand that rotating a shape does not change its angles
✔ Combine right angles to form straight angles
✔ Recognise that straight angles measure 180°
✔ Apply known angle facts when solving problems
✔ Justify their reasoning mathematically

The lesson introduces angles at a point.
Students learn that the angles around any point always total 360°.

Students will:
✔ Use the fact that angles at a point sum to 360°
✔ Find missing angles around a point
✔ Match complementary angle pairs that total 360°
✔ Solve missing-angle reasoning problems
✔ Apply subtraction accurately when calculating unknown angles

Students also learn how to name angles correctly.
They use standard geometrical notation when describing angles.

Students will:
✔ Name angles using three-letter notation
✔ Identify the vertex correctly
✔ Interpret angle notation accurately
✔ Read labelled diagrams
✔ Communicate mathematical reasoning clearly

The lesson concludes with true-or-false reasoning problems involving reflex angles and angles at a point. Students use known angle facts to determine whether mathematical statements are correct and explain their reasoning.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently use rulers and protractors, calculate interior angle sums of polygons, classify angles, solve problems involving angles around a point, and apply correct geometrical notation when naming and reasoning about angles.

lessons.title: Properties of Shapes 2
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students extend their understanding of angle facts by exploring angles on a straight line and vertically opposite angles. They estimate angle sizes, solve missing-angle problems using known angle relationships, and apply logical reasoning to increasingly complex geometrical diagrams.

This lesson includes:
✔ Estimating angle sizes
✔ Solving angles on a straight line
✔ Understanding vertically opposite angles
✔ Calculating missing angles using angle facts
✔ Solving multi-step angle reasoning problems

Students begin by estimating angles before calculating their exact values.

Students will:
✔ Estimate acute, obtuse and reflex angles
✔ Compare angles with right and straight angles
✔ Explain why an estimate is reasonable
✔ Develop stronger visual angle recognition
✔ Build confidence before calculating exact values

The lesson then introduces angles on a straight line.
Students learn that adjacent angles on a straight line always total 180°.

Students will:
✔ Understand that a straight angle measures 180°
✔ Recognise that 180° is half a full turn
✔ Calculate missing angles on a straight line
✔ Use subtraction to solve unknown angles
✔ Apply straight-line angle facts in reasoning questions

Students strengthen this understanding through matching, true-or-false activities and missing-angle problems.

Students will:
✔ Match angle pairs that total 180°
✔ Identify incorrect angle statements
✔ Explain mathematical reasoning
✔ Solve progressively more challenging missing-angle questions
✔ Check answers using known angle facts

The lesson then introduces vertically opposite angles.
Students discover that when two straight lines intersect, opposite angles are always equal.

Students will:
✔ Recognise intersecting lines
✔ Identify pairs of vertically opposite angles
✔ Understand that vertically opposite angles are equal
✔ Calculate missing angles using opposite-angle facts
✔ Combine vertically opposite angles with straight-line reasoning

Students apply multiple angle facts together to solve increasingly complex diagrams.

Students will:
✔ Calculate several missing angles from one given angle
✔ Combine vertically opposite angles with angles on a straight line
✔ Solve complete angle diagrams systematically
✔ Label unknown angles correctly
✔ Justify each step of their reasoning

The lesson concludes with mixed reasoning questions where students combine all of the angle facts learned to calculate every missing angle within complex intersecting-line diagrams.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently estimate angle sizes, solve problems involving angles on a straight line and vertically opposite angles, combine multiple angle facts to calculate unknown angles, and explain their reasoning using correct mathematical vocabulary.

lessons.title: Properties of Shapes 3
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students deepen their understanding of geometrical reasoning by solving increasingly challenging angle problems involving triangles, squares, rectangles, parallel lines and isosceles triangles. They develop fluency in identifying, classifying and reasoning about two-dimensional shapes before exploring the properties of different types of triangles.

Students learn to:

✔ Apply angle facts involving triangles, straight lines, parallel lines and angles around a point
✔ Identify and classify common polygons
✔ Recognise and describe different types of triangles

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently combine multiple angle facts, classify two-dimensional shapes accurately, identify the properties of equilateral, isosceles, scalene and right-angled triangles, and solve increasingly complex geometrical reasoning problems using clear mathematical justification.

lessons.title: Properties of Shapes 4

They investigate the properties of common quadrilaterals, calculate missing angles, explore regular and irregular polygons, calculate perimeters, determine interior angle sums using the polygon formula, and solve increasingly challenging polygon reasoning problems.

Students learn to:
✔ Identify and describe common three-dimensional shapes
✔ Compare and classify quadrilaterals using their properties
✔ Calculate missing angles in quadrilaterals and polygons
✔ Find perimeters of regular and irregular shapes
✔ Use the interior-angle-sum formula for polygons
✔ Solve multi-step polygon reasoning and shape-construction problems

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently classify quadrilaterals and polygons, apply angle and perimeter reasoning, calculate interior angle sums, and solve complex geometrical reasoning problems involving both two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes.

lessons.title: Properties of Shapes 5
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students consolidate their understanding of two-dimensional and three-dimensional geometry through practical drawing tasks, shape construction and advanced reasoning. They draw and complete shapes accurately on grids, explore the properties of three-dimensional shapes, investigate Platonic solids, apply Euler's Rule, interpret shape nets, and solve increasingly challenging spatial reasoning problems.

Students learn to:
✔ Complete and construct two-dimensional shapes accurately
✔ Compare areas and draw shapes on square and isometric grids
✔ Identify faces, edges and vertices of three-dimensional shapes
✔ Understand Platonic solids and apply Euler's Rule
✔ Recognise and evaluate shape nets
✔ Solve advanced three-dimensional reasoning problems involving slicing and combining solids

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently construct accurate geometrical figures, analyse three-dimensional shapes, apply Euler's Rule, interpret shape nets, and solve sophisticated spatial reasoning problems involving faces, edges, vertices and composite solids.

They learn the properties of circles, identify and use the radius, diameter and circumference, discover the relationships between these measurements, solve simple circle algebra problems, and apply their understanding to increasingly challenging real-life reasoning questions.

Students learn to:
✔ Identify and describe the parts of a circle
✔ Understand the relationships between radius, diameter and circumference
✔ Apply simple circle algebra using radius and diameter
✔ Estimate circumference using the diameter
✔ Solve practical circle reasoning problems involving distance and measurement
✔ Apply circle properties in increasingly complex geometrical contexts

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently identify and use the key parts of a circle, calculate missing measurements using the relationships between radius, diameter and circumference, apply simple circle algebra, and solve multi-step reasoning problems involving circles in both mathematical and real-life situations.

lessons.title: Non Standard Partitioning
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students explore non-standard partitioning and composing of large numbers, including numbers with decimals. They learn that numbers can be partitioned in many different ways while maintaining the same value, and they apply non-standard partitioning strategies to calculation, reasoning and problem solving.

This lesson includes:
✔ Standard and non-standard partitioning
✔ Composing numbers from non-standard unit parts
✔ Partitioning numbers in multiple ways
✔ Using non-standard partitioning to support calculations
✔ Solving reasoning and word problems involving place value

Students begin by revisiting standard partitioning and composing numbers from place value parts.

Students will:
✔ Compose numbers from given place value parts
✔ Partition large whole numbers and decimals
✔ Identify the value of each digit
✔ Represent numbers using place value understanding
✔ Explain how numbers are composed and decomposed

The lesson then introduces non-standard partitioning.

Students will:
✔ Understand that numbers can be partitioned in different ways
✔ Split place values into alternative groupings
✔ Combine place values into larger units
✔ Recognise that the total value remains unchanged
✔ Compare standard and non-standard partitioning methods

Students deepen their understanding by creating multiple representations of the same number.

Students will:
✔ Find different non-standard partitions of a number
✔ Explain similarities and differences between partitions
✔ Represent numbers using place value counters and models
✔ Justify why different partitions have the same value
✔ Develop flexible number sense

The lesson then focuses on non-standard composing.

Students will:
✔ Compose numbers from non-standard unit parts
✔ Regroup place value parts efficiently
✔ Combine similar place values mentally
✔ Interpret non-standard representations accurately
✔ Explain their methods clearly

Students apply non-standard partitioning to reasoning and problem-solving contexts.

Students will:
✔ Evaluate whether mathematical statements are correct
✔ Explain errors and justify reasoning
✔ Use part-whole models to solve subtraction problems
✔ Apply partitioning strategies to word problems
✔ Solve place-value puzzles and challenges

The lesson concludes with reasoning activities involving hopscotch pathways and multiple representations of the same number. Students identify valid non-standard partitions and justify their choices using place value knowledge.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently compose and partition numbers using both standard and non-standard methods, understand that numbers can be represented in many equivalent ways, and apply flexible place value strategies to solve reasoning and real-life problems.
